entry.title: Hanwen's WePie Career Chronicle
entry.content:
Shen Hanwen (ShenHanWen / SHW2002) · A review of work and growth, 2024–2026

Shen Hanwen’s time at WePie can be traced back to a fishing UI. At first, the questions were fixed headings and scrolling lists. Later, his records included cross-platform migration, animation synchronization, and code generation. Together they show a gradual expansion of responsibility: finish a feature, make it survive the whole workflow, then prepare reusable foundations for the next development effort and the colleagues taking it over.

In 2024, as internship gave way to graduation, he entered commercial game development. Computers and games had long been interests; joining a team gave those interests concrete form: live versions, assets awaiting integration, requirements to confirm together, and player feedback after release. Neverland (梦幻岛), Hide and Seek (躲猫猫), and Sunny Island (《小岛有晴天》) each contributed a different experience. Across them, he learned to solve immediate problems more completely and leave the solutions behind.

1 · 2024–2025 · Neverland: building business foundations in a mature project

Neverland was an important starting point. Its rich gameplay and accumulated rules required a newcomer to learn while working. Hanwen began with UI, interaction, and presentation issues, gradually contributing to fishing progression, tackle, and vehicles as connected feature groups. His annual review singled out Neverland 2.6 going live on WePlay’s Chinese-language service: his first experience contributing to development and following a release all the way through. Players’ enthusiasm gave direct feedback. Completing that first delivery made the lesson concrete at every entry point: after a button press, server data, UI, and character state must all support the result.

1.1 Fishing and vehicles: from a first release to clear state responsibilities

  • Complete a first launch: contribute to fishing development in Neverland 2.6 and its Chinese-language release, building experience from requirements through deployment.

  • Distinguish character states: separate “in a vehicle” from “driving,” establishing boundaries for passenger movement, driving, and leaving a boat.

    • isInVehicle and isDriving represent boarding and driving separately. Driving requires already being aboard; leaving also exits driving.
    • Camera and movement modules subscribe to the relevant state changes, integrating passenger and driver behavior through separate interfaces.

Much of this learning happened in ordinary exchanges. For the fish-basket UI, he checked navigation, fixed regions, scrolling, and sizing with a UI designer, used existing screens to clarify behavior, and confirmed the implemented result, earning the designer’s approval. Similar distinctions in vehicles became state interfaces and module responsibilities. The progress lay in specifics: first understand how one screen should be used, then distinguish how several gameplay systems share one character.

1.2 Refactoring GM tools: extensible commands that are easy to find

As fishing and vehicles expanded, the team’s debug commands grew. Developers and testers needed to locate business operations quickly and keep common ones in fixed places. Hanwen organized these needs into a new GM tool. It brought operations from different features together for daily debugging, reproduction, and verification. Its use spread beyond developers as collaboration broadened.


Neverland · Excerpt from the GM categories and favorites panel

  • Give commands a common home: register categories and commands at runtime, reusing the same panel presentation and execution flow as gameplay expands.

    • Extract command management from NLGMPanel into NLGMTool, representing names, categories, and execution functions as registrable data.
    • Generate lists centrally and record results and errors consistently; business modules add commands in the same way.

  • Keep common operations close at hand: add favorites that survive restarts. Testers confirmed that finding and explaining entry points became easier and suggested similar improvements for Sunny Island.

    • Store favorites using command-name keys, restore them on startup, reject duplicates, and clean persistent storage after removal.
    • Improve handover through development-team trials and tester instructions, bringing favorites and categories into daily debugging.

From command organization and panel integration to persistence, Hanwen delivered a complete tool colleagues could use, then improved it through trials, instructions, and feedback. It was an early lesson in delivery: an improvement he proposed and implemented must also work in somebody else’s day. Shared registration helped developers add commands, while other roles could find the operations they needed. Daily use confirmed the tool’s value.

1.3 The first Unity Autorun: automate repeated game-entry steps

Entering the game meant a familiar sequence: run the editor, wait for scene loading, connect services, and enter gameplay. These stable, repeated steps offered a clear automation target. Autorun began there, letting presets take over fixed operations while developers used loading time for other work. The small tool turned repeated daily actions into a reusable workflow.

  • Automate repetitive clicks: entering Neverland previously involved about 30 seconds of waiting and manual operations; presets took over the clicking portion.

    • Presets record button names or text, UI types, and waits, execute them in sequence, and support exit steps before stopping a run.

  • Grow from one project to three: saved configurations cover three projects—Neverland, the store, and Hide and Seek—with real entry and exit steps.

    • Save settings by project and configure them through a GUI; add tutorials responding to colleagues’ confusion and disable Run for empty presets.

After handover, he actively asked about difficulties and updated the tutorial for configuring a freshly checked-out project and using the GUI. Trial discussions gradually improved configuration, documentation, and guidance, making the tool easier to use in colleagues’ own projects. It later crossed into Sunny Island and evolved into a navigation graph. The early settings, documentation, and feedback began that thread.

1.4 Migrating Neverland fishing and vehicles: toward complete delivery

Moving fishing and vehicles from the Chinese-language service to Huiwan took the work beyond the familiar project. Native capabilities, backend connectivity, and interactions between boarding and Huiwan-specific flight or other gameplay all needed confirmation. Hanwen organized call relationships, test scope, and remaining work, then coordinated priorities, support, and regression with the team. Previously focused on feature implementation, he now saw how a release passed between roles on its way to production.

  • All 83 checks passed: that round of vehicle smoke testing for Neverland 2.7 contained 83 cases, all 83 passing—a 100% pass rate, confirmed by a tester in the project group.

    • Trace Unity calls to native clients and backends, identifying exact methods and endpoints for item previews, friends, rewards, and image loading.
    • Add verification priorities for flight, room changes, boarding, and wedding-island boundaries around vehicle room relationships and local coordinates.

  • One fewer request for reward indicators: the pre-refresh path for album reward badges reduced proactive CollectOverview requests from one per refresh to zero, reusing existing pushes.

    • Confirm album data already arrives by push, then remove the duplicate request before badge evaluation. The business module owns seasonal click records; the general layer owns nodes and visibility conditions.
    • Include refresh after acquisition, redemption, use, and gifting in verification, delivering both optimization and checking requirements.

Migration preparation connected interfaces, gameplay, and verification. Knowledge from the old environment became checks he could explain in the new one. He also actively performed Code Review in related versions, bringing his implementations into shared inspection. Testing, regression, and launch then followed explicit priorities. He progressed from contributing features to organizing delivery of his own area, translating technical judgment into plans the team could execute.

Badge optimization followed the same approach. Clear ownership of business rules and shared capabilities produced clearer interfaces; fewer requests came with explicit verification of refresh behavior. The optimization included both implementation and checks, so collaborators knew what changed and what to inspect. These practices became habits when maintaining existing features.

  • Integrate new vehicles through a shared process: organize asset configuration, type-specific rules, and exit flow separately, supported by an editor and authoring instructions.

    • Configure position, actions, and camera per asset; vehicle types implement rules such as sitting on a jet ski.
    • Use ExitContext and prepareExitVehicle to connect standing, leaving driver mode, and disembarking, documenting and teaching the workflow.

Vehicle expansion extended these lessons into asset production. Editors, documentation, and group explanations handed code conventions to artists, giving model, animation, and camera preparation a common process. The output now included interfaces for subsequent vehicles and authoring instructions users could follow. Development considered both how features run and how other roles continue creating content.

1.5 Log cleanup: finding removable cost in high-frequency output

After business implementation, Hanwen began looking at runtime behavior. Debug logs revealed execution, and organizing them by purpose and frequency became a concrete optimization direction. He sampled from game entry, ranked frequent sources, explained retaining important network/resource information at a development meeting, and pushed prioritized release of the changes. Optimization started by understanding what was happening.

  • Quiet more than nine hundred repeated logs: in a sample from entering Neverland until five seconds after frame-rate stabilization, one message appeared over 900 times. He recorded noticeably improved smoothness after removing it.

    • Locate frequent sources by count, retain key network/resource diagnostics, and prioritize releasing the relevant changes.
    • Add a default-off debug switch to badge tooling and log tags, then continue organizing shared loading, network, and character output.

This extended into routine maintenance: control output according to need while preserving diagnostic switches for investigation. Several Neverland work streams now converged—business implementation, tooling, and runtime observation supported a live system together. Hanwen increasingly looked beyond feature completion to how it ran, leaving reusable maintenance practices for the next development round.

2 · Late 2024 to early 2025 · Hide and Seek: real-time gameplay and multiplayer synchronization

While Neverland continued iterating, Hanwen joined Hide and Seek. Built on the earlier Ao Oni project, it could reuse assets but needed reorganized rules. His focus shifted toward characters: movement, collision, camera, and animation must cooperate in one operation, and other clients must see the result after a local button press. Learning old code and establishing new rules happened together, bringing boundary decisions into the core of real-time gameplay.

2.1 Real-time gameplay: adapt flow and character behavior to new rules


Hide and Seek · Counterattack trajectory development and debugging

  • Adapt the main flow and capture behavior: contribute phase flow, pursuer AI, and counterattack skills, integrating movement detection, pursuit, freezing, and human/AI control changes.

    • AI tracks nearby surviving players, pursues when movement triggers it, and returns to patrol after a timeout; freezing, stun, and human-control states consistently constrain behavior.
    • Retain existing position synchronization while implementing counterattack ascent/descent in model presentation. Validate charging locally, play remotely from release messages, and handle early collision cleanup.

  • A large test with zero bugs: according to the designer’s review, the final large-scale test found zero bugs. Test updates also confirmed version 1.0 testing was complete and quality stable.

These divisions translated rules into character behavior and gave local input, remote presentation, and control handover distinct responsibilities. Development required understanding the existing framework and selecting suitable places for new rules; integration required checking message/state relationships with the server team. Movement, presentation, and input became clearer, letting the existing project support new real-time gameplay.

Hanwen worked with his mentor and another client developer. Designers and testers recognized the stable stage-test results. While still gaining full-project experience, he learned that inherited framework constraints could still support delivery through clear responsibilities. The experience later reappeared in Sunny Island’s separation of local decisions from remote presentation: projects changed, but carefully understood problems remained useful.

2.2 Lua annotations: from cross-language needs to upstream contribution

A tooling thread continued across projects. Neverland and Hide and Seek both used Lua and C#, making reliable cross-language hints an everyday concern. Hanwen first asked his mentor how editors recognize annotations, then modified type generation and organized real needs into an existing open-source generator. He grew from a configuration user into a contributor able to repair and extend the tool.


EmmyLua annotation generator · GitHub repository and README excerpts · 2026-09-22

  • Bring project patches upstream: six categories of capabilities, including generic inference, aliases, and function compatibility, were merged through PR #2. Project adaptations became part of the original tool’s public version.

    • Refine common generic inheritance so members such as Singleton<T>.Instance receive useful hints; express C# delegate/Lua function compatibility through union types.
    • Split annotation files, save generation options, and document language-service directories and compatibility settings for repeated practical use.

Real project calls guided the changes, and usage gradually filled out the instructions. The repository went to colleagues for trials before upstream submission, connecting generation, editor settings, and public maintenance. The merge was a concrete result; the lasting change was that a local solution, once organized, could serve other developers and build his open-source collaboration experience.

3 · Late 2025–2026 · Sunny Island: from character control to synchronization architecture

Sunny Island brought a substantial change in responsibility. His annual review described his first complete ownership of a game module from the ground up: designing, implementing, and iterating 3C within the existing framework, organizing character, camera, and controls into foundations for future gameplay. Requirements sometimes began as reference videos. He analyzed controls, built playable versions to align with designers, then organized synchronization, configuration, and assets. Earlier experience became a sustained area of ownership.

3.1 First full 3C ownership: exploration through continued delivery

  • Own the core module’s whole cycle: from reference analysis and playable validation to implementation and iteration, continue building Sunny Island’s 3C.

    • Make an experiential version first, check controls and presentation with designers, then implement confirmed rules in character and animation systems.
    • Refine interfaces and settings for new content so the module supports later personal actions and complex interactions.

  • Reproduce playback remotely: use StateNameHash, continuous parameters, and NextState for state passthrough, with generated ClipOnly controllers, forming reusable synchronization for subsequent personal actions.

    • Make decisions locally and play remotely from state information; generate ClipOnly controllers from the same source machine while retaining necessary automatic exits.
    • Pre-blend through NextState, collect requests by layer, read states one frame later, and identify replay using playback time.


ClipOnly controller generator · GitHub README excerpt · 2026-09-22

  • Document the technical result: write “Implementing Animation Synchronization with Pass-Through States in Unity Mecanim,” including scope and supporting tools.

    • Explain suitability for small social scenes, the design’s evolution, and companion generators for later reference and reuse.

Animation synchronization became a representative outcome of complete ownership. Later actions reused it; asset changes had generation support; the implementation and boundaries became an article. His own design kept serving new content, strengthening his grasp of the core module: make technical choices, deliver them, and maintain them through real use.

3.2 Export tooling and conventions: encode experience in generation rules

Once he owned a core module, peripheral work deserved earlier organization too. More settings meant accumulating costs from handwritten IDs, copied generation scripts, and collisions. The Neverland habit of tooling repeated operations reached the connection between data and code in Sunny Island. Fixing a table keeps today’s version moving; generation rules also provide a way to integrate the next table.

  • Eight output flows, one maintenance point: consolidate eight repetitive C# output flows into one shared implementation, used by six generator types and then NPCs, covering seven types in total.

    • Extend Luban with ItemId constants, standardizing system/name/ID references; validate enums and append IDs with warnings for duplicate names.
    • Centralize parameter checks, structure, comments, and output in UGFIdGeneratorBase; discover and run generators together while retaining each table’s reading and naming rules.
    • Skip unchanged writes, reuse shared naming steps, and integrate new types such as NPCs through the same flow.

The growth was in turning personal maintenance experience into project rules. Generated names standardized references, generation checked enums and collisions, and common output had one owner. Conventions gained an executable form that later types could reuse. Early tooling habits became engineering foundations: a solution from one task became a condition already available for the team’s next task.

3.3 From completion to quality delivery: implementation, self-tests, and handover

Personal-action delivery tested both architecture and working methods. After playback, synchronization, and configuration, Hanwen ran smoke cases and documented completion, asset arrangements, verification, and later integration points. Module ownership covered implementation, self-testing, integration, and testing handover. Leads and testers could plan from these records, while designers could continue adding content through existing settings.


Animation metadata generator · GitHub README and generation examples · 2026-09-22

  • Update assets and code together: generate layer, parameter, and state definitions alongside ClipOnly controllers. Invalid references can surface at compilation while asset relationships remain preserved.

    • Generate enums and constants for layers, parameters, and states, handling special characters, keywords, and duplicate identifiers.
    • Regenerate code and remote controllers from source assets; publish the tools alongside the synchronization article.

  • Integrate new actions through configuration: designers can configure supported actions once assets are ready, while programmers maintain playback and synchronization centrally.

    • Replace clips in fixed state structures through AnimatorOverrideController; configure freezing, interruption, blending, and layer redirection.
    • Expose one business interface through different drivers: local parameter updates and remote state changes, with Entity-managed lifecycles.

  • Maintain quality as content grows: stage reports recorded fewer than ten bugs after over 90% of personal-action cases had been tested. For new tools in Sunny Island 0.7, excluding missing-configuration issues, functional smoke tests passed 100%, earning specific praise from testers.

    • Organize held, placement-preview, and placed entities separately, clarifying asset responsibilities, settings, and acceptance requirements.
    • Self-test before handover and state completed features and missing resources clearly, letting design, art, and testing proceed from one explanation.

These responses marked a shift from assigned-task completion to responsibility for delivery. Stage self-tests, clear asset handover, and follow-up gave his modules complete closure; low stage defect counts and tester approval provided practical feedback. Animation tools and authoring instructions continued serving later versions. Independent ownership grew through implementation, verification, and handover.

3.4 Authoring conventions: deliver technical systems as team workflows

From Neverland’s vehicle editor to Sunny Island’s Timeline, Hanwen increasingly considered implementation and user handover together. He saved Timeline binding data and restored runtime references, then documented authoring, saving, reloading, and acceptance. Code supplied capability; documentation explained order and responsibilities so designers, artists, and programmers could proceed. Technical experience became a repeatable team process.

  • Deliver bindings and authoring instructions: own track-target persistence, runtime restoration, and supporting documentation, connecting asset creation with code integration.

    • Save target hierarchy paths and object/component types, restore references at runtime, and reuse a scene object index.
    • Distinguish scene references from prefab-internal objects; explain when to save bindings and how to resave and reload after changes.

  • Include acceptance in authoring: put operations, handover, and expected runtime results in one usable reference.

    • Explain requirements such as restoring camera control afterward, so creators know what to check beyond the visible effect.
    • Document held, preview, and placed entity responsibilities, configuration relationships, and minimum acceptance checks.

His responsibility had expanded. Earlier he asked colleagues to clarify UI and asset rules; now he explained tools and delivery himself. Vehicle documentation and group teaching grew into more complete operation and acceptance instructions. His output included steps other roles could follow and references for handling specific situations, beyond code alone.

3.5 Collection displays and newcomer collaboration: supporting shared delivery

The collection feature displayed existing characters and crops in a new way. Combining characters with enlarged crops made size, pose, and loading order significant. Unexpectedly tiny characters led investigation into skinning and bones. Reusing the team’s scene entities, Hanwen handled concentrated technical display work while a newcomer developed the main collection feature. He was now finishing key modules while supporting someone else’s development.


Sunny Island · Excerpt from a 3D collection display

  • Fit combined models into the display: organize pose, bounds measurement, and scaling after clothing and held items are ready, supporting different resource combinations.

    • Wait for clothing, items, skinning updates, and a stable pose before measuring current world bounds.
    • Exclude hidden parts and particles; scale uniformly using the most restrictive axis for characters combined with oversized crops.

  • Extend beyond one display: colleagues extended the collection-leaderboard animation driver into two later areas—wish-privilege previews and team-event rankings.

    • AnimDriverScenePlayer reuses clip loading, caching, and overrides while separating display poses from real player control.
    • Separate “retrieve actual clothing” from “load a model by slot,” enabling wish try-ons and other display features.

  • Share development experience with a newcomer: alongside his display module, participate in collection code review, protocol guidance, and test preparation.

    • Explain using generated PB structures and compiling after generation before committing, establishing consistent data integration.
    • Review collection detail pages, share findings, and guide UI state organization and early communication about dependencies.
    • Confirm configuration, self-test, and integration progress; include review and smoke verification in test preparation.

His responsibility now included shared delivery. The newcomer drove main functionality while Hanwen handled 3D presentation, requirements checks, support, and review; the lead asked him to keep following the newcomer’s work. From asking a mentor to explaining interfaces and integration to a newcomer, the role changed through concrete collaboration. He began explaining his judgment and bringing code checks, configuration, and handover into shared progress.

3.6 Project self-test tooling: from startup presets to offline UI navigation

The early automatic-click tool returned to the story in Sunny Island. Initially meant to reduce waiting through loading, it grew as more projects and screens made reaching a test entry point repetitive work. Autorun evolved from sequential presets into a UI navigation graph: prepare routes once and reuse them in later self-tests. An early tooling habit found a wider scope.


Unity Autorun MCP · Public application interface excerpt · 2026-09-22

  • Save traveled routes for later tests: the project had 54 configured routes, and editor buttons and command lines reused prepared paths.

    • Generate and check paths to target screens in advance, execute through editor or CLI, and expose task-state queries.

  • Run daily navigation independently: offline execution of a generated graph requires zero AI inference calls. AI participates in preparation and later updates.

    • Provide external operations through a local HTTP Bridge and separate MCP Server, separating route preparation from repeated execution.
    • Share installation and offline navigation instructions with the team and technical community, maintaining them from real test feedback.

Autorun followed practical work from personal use to colleague installation and public maintenance. Separating preparation from repetition made familiar entries reusable; instructions let more users join the flow. An early automation need became a continuously evolving tool, linking several projects through one habit that gradually took on a broader role.

3.7 Complex movement and two-player interaction: transport, pose, and timing

Rope movement, hand-holding, and intimate actions made the character system coordinate more at once. One person’s turn must be followed by the other’s position, hands, and animation, while observers receive data on their own schedule. Animation drivers, state boundaries, resource lifecycles, and networking converged in one experience. Hanwen separated stutter, misalignment, and joint twitching, located their causes, then made the fixes cooperate toward continuous motion.

  • Slow rope snapshot transmission: the minimum interval increased from 50 ms to 100 ms, changing nominal frequency from 20 Hz to 10 Hz—a 50% reduction. Receivers retained interpolation and short extrapolation.

    • Return special-gameplay scheduling to the shared character interval, leaving continuous presentation to receivers and maintaining transport separately from visual processing.


Sunny Island · Two-player interaction development

Rope tradeoffs extended into two-person interaction. Hand-holding needs stable shared position and pose while leaving room to tune different actions. Hanwen separated shared contact, turning follow, and joint pose, established their calculation and update order, then integrated them into one flow. Experience adjustments now corresponded to specific mechanisms, and new resources could follow existing rules.

  • Three issues resolved the same day: his update to the lead reported three bugs found in that test round after the initial experience, with those and smoke-test findings fixed that day.

  • Start and end paired actions together: each client prepares both players’ resources, then applies both positions and actions on the same local frame, handling messages and cleanup by relationship ID, sequence, and phase.

    • Separate resource waiting from playback timing; check relationship IDs, sequence, and phase to reject stale data.
    • Restore positions, remove relationships, and clean Timeline through common phases for entry and exit.

  • Adapt contact and joints together: the initiator controls following and IK targets, with independent shoulder, elbow, and wrist constraints and smoothing.

    • Retain a reference pose for the interaction, smooth a shared contact point in initiator-local space, and apply reachability constraints and asset offsets.
    • Tune turn lag, angular speed, and follow speed separately while preserving ordinary movement rhythm.
    • Reference upper arms to the character and elbows/wrists to parent bones; constrain yaw, pitch, and roll separately and cache final constrained rotations as the next smoothing baseline.

Experience kept shaping the implementation after initial delivery. Preparation, execution, and cleanup gained common phases, while constraints and smoothing became clearer through iteration. Communication and closed requirements recorded the results. Reachable contact, reasonable joints, and complete exit now had distinct mechanisms, giving collaborators boundaries for confirming requirements and tuning the interaction.

  • Smooth locally, transmit less often: periodic paired-pose transmission changed from 30 ms to 100 ms, nominally about 33.3 Hz to 10 Hz—a 70% reduction. Hand IK changed from 30 ms to 200 ms, reaching 5 Hz—an 85% reduction.

    • Place both poses in one sampled snapshot; recipients and observers interpolate along the same timeline. Brief gaps allow bounded extrapolation; teleportation or long gaps rebuild the baseline.
    • Let the initiator calculate and smooth animation speed every frame, with different start/stop thresholds and independent pose, animation, and IK intervals.
    • Self-tests against a non-local server recorded smoother motion, and the straight-line stutter item was subsequently closed.

The results have support in experience feedback, implementation, and transmission settings. Positions, joints, and animation parameters are smoothed separately; network cadence is independently adjustable. Together they create continuous paired presentation. His approach grew from individual fixes into organizing calculation, transport, and playback as a whole. Earlier character-system experience formed a more complete cooperation within this complex interaction.

Afterword: make one delivery the starting point for the next

The growth follows a clear path. Neverland taught commercial development and collaboration through fishing, vehicles, and complete tool delivery. Hide and Seek focused his attention on real-time gameplay and multiplayer synchronization. In Sunny Island, these experiences joined a 3C module under sustained ownership. From understanding systems to choosing designs, implementing, self-testing, and iterating, he learned to own a module completely and leave reusable foundations for later content.

Quality and collaboration gave technical progress concrete responses: stable stage tests, colleague approval, reuse in later business features, and upstream acceptance of open-source improvements. He also documented authoring, encoded naming and validation rules, reviewed code, and supported newcomers. More people could understand and use his methods, extending personal responsibility into shared delivery.


HanWen / SHW2002 · GitHub profile · 2026-09-22

This review stops here for now; exploration continues. The past few years now form experience he can draw on: clarify rules, build the design, verify results, and hand the method to its next user. A finished feature leaves code. Careful delivery leaves quality and trust; organizing those experiences gives the next task a better starting point. That is what “building the world a little at a time” means in this part of his career.

Sources: This article draws on Git commits from Neverland, Hide and Seek, and Sunny Island; personal technical documentation and annual reviews; Feishu text discussions and requirement records; and SHW2002’s public GitHub contributions, with material collected through September 21, 2026. Key figures come from corresponding test feedback, sampling records, and code configuration.

entry.title: An Unattended All-in-One Timelapse Workflow
entry.content:
I built an automated workflow around TimelapseManager: configure the camera, dependencies, and schedule, then create a task to capture brackets, download photos, fuse HDR, deflicker, and export video.

Optional sunset scoring finds colorful intervals, rates albums, and sends results through WeCom.

The tools now support one-off, daily recurring, and continuous batch tasks. Capture, HDR fusion, and scoring can run concurrently, and background tasks continue after the management window closes. This article focuses on the outputs and the task model, image processing, and recovery design behind the automation.

The overview puts tasks, states, current stages, and workers in one interface. It comes from the repository’s UI demonstration; task data is illustrative.

1. One task produces a video and selectable source material

For a fixed camera recording dusk, I want the program to perform these operations after I set the schedule:

CapabilityResult
Scheduled capture and downloadLocal photo sequences numbered by exposure group
Exposure fusion and deflickeringFused HDR frames and brightness-smoothed video input
Video encodingAn H.265-encoded MP4 timelapse
Optional sunset analysisScores and reasons per sample, the highest-scoring photo, and sunset intervals
Archiving and notificationsAlbums organized by date and time, maximum-score directory labels, and text/image notifications

Suppose a task runs from 16:00 to 20:00, capturing a three-photo group every six seconds. Ideally it produces about 2,400 groups and 7,200 JPGs. Fusing each group into one frame and encoding at 30 fps compresses four hours into about 80 seconds. These are material-count and duration estimates; exposure, download time, and interruptions affect the actual frame count.

Video and album output

A completed, cleaned, and archived task with a maximum sunset score of 4 might retain:

This is an illustrative structure. hdr_enfuse holds fused frames, hdr_video holds the video, and the score file retains analysis. S4 on date and time directories makes valuable periods visible in the file manager. When several marked albums share a day, the outer date directory uses their maximum score.

Processing also produces original exposure groups and intermediate hdr_deflick frames. Task cleanup settings determine whether to retain them, allowing direct video review while keeping HDR sequences worth further editing.

Sunset selection results

These actual SunsetScore examples come from the same timelapse sequence. Ordinary white/gray clouds score 1, softer colored clouds score 3, and widespread vivid cloud coloring scores 4.

Original score labels are retained, arranged from low to high. This example set contains no score-5 photo.

For daily fixed-camera recording, selection reduces opening folders and searching frame by frame for sunset color. The video supports a quick review; scores and intervals identify material worth a closer look.

2. Architecture: one entry point, specialized tools

All projects live in the GitHub Hanwen Photograph organization. TimelapseManager offers both GUI and CLI; its repository is still named Timelapse-Auto-Script.

Manager schedules tasks, manages processes, aggregates progress, and handles results. Specialized tools perform image processing, connected through command lines, files, and public event protocols:

flowchart TB    UI["TimelapseManager GUI / CLI"] --> M["Task service and background workers<br/>Configuration, scheduling, processes, logs"]    M -->|Launch and monitor| C["Camera Timelapse Controller<br/>Camera control with gphoto2"]    M -->|Launch and monitor| B["Bracketlapse<br/>Optional alignment and enfuse fusion"]    C -->|Complete stable exposure groups| B    B -->|HDR sequence| D["Simple Deflicker<br/>Brightness deflickering"]    D --> V["FFmpeg<br/>H.265 video"]    B -->|hdr_ready forwarded by Manager| S["SunsetScore<br/>Persistent local scoring service"]    S --> A["Manager result handling<br/>Album labels, HDR retention, notifications"]

Bracketlapse organizes exposure fusion, deflickering, and encoding; SunsetScore handles directory sampling, model inference, and score aggregation. Manager coordinates through public interfaces. Each tool can run independently, and its internals can be replaced or improved.

Lumalapse and NEF Filter provide separate paths for detailed RAW editing and organization after selection. They are currently used independently. The main capture pipeline directly connects camera control, Bracketlapse, and SunsetScore; Simple Deflicker participates as a Bracketlapse post-processing dependency.

3. Task management: keeping one-click startup running

Presets create explicit tasks

Manager offers four creation presets for ad hoc capture, daily schedules, and long-term recording:

PresetUse caseExecution
manualA specified day and time windowSet directory, start/end dates and times, and capture interval
scheduled_onceThe next morning or duskGenerate one task from project settings
scheduled_loopDaily repeated captureAutomatically create and start a successor after each run
eternalContinuous recordingArchive complete exposure groups in batches and process them sequentially in the background

Scheduled presets expand into explicit manual tasks at creation; looping presets also carry task-chain information. Each run has its own time range, directory, status, and logs, so problems can be traced to one capture.

Continuous mode divides material into batches of complete exposure groups. Capture keeps producing photos while the background processes archived batches. Group boundaries prevent the three photos of one exposure set from landing in different directories.

Separate the interface from execution

GUI and CLI share a task service; independent background workers perform capture. Definitions and runtime state are persisted separately:

Closing the GUI does not stop capture. Reopening restores monitoring and control. Startup validates settings and dependencies; a startup lock and task-state checks prevent duplicate launches.

Stopping has several meanings: end capture early and process existing material, stop after the current task or batch, or stop immediately. During dusk recording, these choices create different material and processing boundaries; they cannot all be reduced to terminating a process.

4. Image processing: from brackets to stable timelapse frames

Exposure groups connect capture and processing

Camera Timelapse Controller uses gphoto2. By default it captures three brackets using the camera’s configured AEB mode; it also supports manual exposure-compensation changes for individual shots.

The Nikon Z30 settings photo from Bracketlapse shows where to configure three-shot bracketing; values are examples.

Downloads use “group number + member number,” such as 0001_01.jpg, 0001_02.jpg, and 0001_03.jpg. An existing directory can resume from its largest group number. This naming also gives post-processing an explicit grouping protocol.

Bracketlapse accepts a group only when members 01 through N are complete and files remain stable across successive scans. Temporary downloads such as captXXXX.jpg and incomplete groups are ignored. A missing photo in one group does not prevent later group numbers from being processed.

processing.group_size defines N, falling back to eternal.images_per_group when not set separately. It must match the actual number of captured photos.

Include capture and download time in the interval

The capture interval is the target gap between successive group start times. For six seconds, if capture and download take three seconds, wait about three more. If they already exceed six seconds, log a warning and start the next group immediately.

This avoids waiting an additional fixed six seconds after every capture and drifting from the configured cadence. Camera and transfer speed still limit throughput; a smaller setting does not guarantee equally spaced photos at that interval.

Fusion, deflickering, and encoding have different roles

Bracketlapse uses Hugin’s enfuse to combine exposures into a frame with more suitable highlights and shadows. Optional align_image_stack alignment handles slight camera movement.

Exposure fusion handles tonal choices within one frame. Timelapse playback also needs inter-frame brightness consistency. Simple Deflicker builds brightness histograms, derives target distributions with a moving average, then uses histogram matching to smooth global flicker while accommodating the gradual change of sunset.

This work maintains a fork of struffel/simple-deflicker, adding histogram smoothing adjustments, CLI builds, and macOS support. It handles global JPG/PNG brightness flicker, not rolling bands from indoor lights.

FFmpeg finally creates an H.265 MP4 from deflickered frames. “HDR” here describes the fused bracketed imagery. HDR10 or HLG video output depends on the color and encoding pipeline; enfuse and H.265 alone do not establish it.

5. A parallel pipeline: capture, fuse, and score concurrently

Completed groups can enter processing immediately during long captures. Bracketlapse’s in-place standby mode keeps a listener running and emits a standard-output event after every fusion:

This says an HDR frame is available. Manager submits a scan request to SunsetScore’s persistent JSONL service; that service scans the directory and processes only new photos at sampling positions. For example:

Submitting scan does not wait for all scoring to finish, so capture and fusion continue. At task completion, Manager sends finalize and waits for final scanning, aggregation, and score-file writing. Sessions distinguish directories; a task and its continuous batches reuse a persistent model, reducing repeated process startup and model loading.

There are two processing granularities: complete exposure groups can be fused and scored incrementally, while deflickering and final video encoding finish after HDR production ends. Scoring can overlap processing completion; final material handling uses the complete result.

Progress comes from actual stage results

Capture, HDR, scoring, and video maintain separate progress. Video uses FFmpeg video_started, video_progress, and video_completed events containing finished and total frame counts. Completion is emitted only after a successful exit.

The interface can therefore show that capture is ongoing, how many HDR groups are done, and how many frames are encoded. Throughput still depends on exposure, downloads, CPU/GPU, and disk. Parallelism reduces waiting without promising a fixed real-time processing speed.

6. Local visual scoring and material retention

From individual scores to sunset intervals

SunsetScore uses a local Qwen3-VL model with llama.cpp. The model selects visual categories; the program maps them to scores from 0 to 5 to keep scores and reasons aligned. After initial resource preparation, scoring can run offline.

The default interval is ten photos: samples 1, 11, 21, 31, and so on. Scores mainly describe visible cloud coloration. Ordinary white clouds, a sunset alone, or a warm horizon do not meet the colorful-cloud threshold. Clearly colored clouds can reach 3; stronger color or wider coverage scores higher.

Any sample reaching 3 produces has_sunset = true. Adjacent high-scoring samples form intervals, split by low scores or failures. Average and maximum scores describe the result; the maximum also labels the album.

Using any clear sample as evidence preserves short-lived color. Hours of ordinary sky should not dilute a few worthwhile minutes. Sampling can still miss shorter changes, so adjust the interval to the capture cadence.

The score describes visual features, not probability or a photograph’s overall value. The model does not read location or EXIF time, so visually similar dawn clouds can also score highly.

Make scores produce explainable archive decisions

Manager uses analysis to decide HDR retention:

ResultHandling
Colorful sunset detectedRetain hdr_enfuse; append the maximum -Sx score to managed date/time albums
Successful scoring without a sunsetMark hdr_enfuse and clean it after three days
Analysis failed, or failed samples exist without a detected sunsetRetain HDR and report scoring failure

Directories without a sunset receive .timelapse-hdr-enfuse-delete with a timezone-aware deadline. Manager scans auto_root on service initialization and later task-list checks, at most once a minute. It handles only valid, expired markers on hdr_enfuse. If no checks run during that period, deletion occurs during a later check.

The three-day window allows review and separate saving. This policy covers only marked HDR directories. Original photos, deflickered intermediate frames, and video follow their respective task cleanup settings.

7. Recovery, dependencies, and notifications for long runs

Keep captured material when processing fails

Capture, processing, and task completion are distinct states. If Bracketlapse exits unexpectedly during a finite capture, Manager records recovery as needed, lets the camera finish, and reruns recovery processing over the final photos with overwrite enabled.

If the finite task still fails, cleanup is skipped and originals retained. Scoring failure must likewise not count as “no sunset,” or inference faults become deletion criteria. These rules protect material before declaring task success.

After a successful download, the camera-control tool deletes the corresponding camera copy. The local download directory therefore owns original preservation, making failure and cleanup boundaries particularly important.

Make task dependencies identifiable

Manager stores workflow tools, Python environments, and scoring resources under the application’s .timelapse/dependencies/. Tasks resolve commands there, reducing differences from global PATH and other Python environments.

The Package Management page checks and installs components. For our tools exposing build information, it shows version, source branch, and build time. Camera Timelapse Controller, Bracketlapse, and SunsetScore updates can select branches, helping identify the exact tool versions a task used.

The GUI supports Windows, macOS, and Linux. Actual camera control depends on gphoto2 support for that camera and platform. The current main flow requires Bracketlapse 0.4.1 or later and optional SunsetScore 0.12.0 or later.

Review results away from the computer

A WeCom webhook sends task states, score summaries, and the highest-scoring photo. Logs diagnose the process, while notifications bring completed results to the place where I normally check messages.

The page supports text and image tests; the robot address uses a YOUR_KEY placeholder.

8. Configure once and reuse

First prepare camera-control and processing components in Package Management. For scoring, also prepare SunsetScore and model resources. Confirm directories and schedules in Configuration Center, then use Task Management to create and start tasks.

Key project settings are shown below; retain other fields from the program’s complete generated configuration:

Morning and dusk are fixed configured windows and should be adjusted by season and location. eternal.batch_groups controls continuous batch size; finite scheduled tasks use start/end times for their capture range.

For everyday use, scheduled_loop chains morning and dusk tasks. Use scheduled_once for only the next run and manual for a particular day and time. The CLI can inspect the environment and background status:

9. Two companion tools: detailed editing and RAW organization

Lumalapse provides RAW sequence import, exposure curves, keyframe color grading, and video export for material needing detailed adjustments. It decodes in linear space through LibRaw/rawpy, computes curves in the log2 brightness domain, and uses the difference between the smoothed target and measured curves as per-frame EV compensation, then adds manual keyframe exposure adjustments.

This combines deflickering with deliberately designed brightness changes while retaining highlight, shadow, and white-balance controls. Analysis and keyframes are cached in the material directory’s .lumalapse/ for reopening and continued editing.

NEF Filter applies JPG selection to Nikon RAW files: it finds NEFs without matching JPGs, displays the proposed deletion list, and waits for confirmation by default. It supports separate JPG and NEF directories and scans non-recursively by default, fitting post-selection organization.

Both are independent companion tools. The automated main flow handles capture through initial selection; worthwhile material can continue into more detailed editing and organization.

10. Evolution and version references

The implementation passed through three main stages: individual camera-control, bracket-fusion, and deflickering capabilities in June; a task manager, GUI, and scoring entry point in July; and incremental processing, persistent models, recovery, and delayed cleanup in August–September. Three choices summarize the resulting design: exchange complete exposure groups, record execution as independent tasks, and base archiving on explicit processing results.

The following versions correspond to this article and support interface checks and configuration reproduction:

ProjectReference version
TimelapseManager / Timelapse-Auto-Script134ddef
Camera Timelapse Controller510c200
Bracketlapse3a6bf7d
Lumalapse58d5192
Simple Deflicker maintained fork6981a61
NEF Filter95ded14
SunsetScore0cdce29

UI screenshots come from TimelapseManager documentation images, the camera photo from Bracketlapse resources, and scoring examples from SunsetScore example images. Local illustrations only undergo format conversion, resizing, and side-by-side layout.

entry.title: Implementing Network-Synchronized Two-Player Hand-Holding in a Game
entry.content:
I developed hand-holding for our social game’s 3C system: the initiator leads and the recipient follows. Both must adapt to terrain, keep their hands together, and work with personal actions and other gameplay.

Hand-holding integration test, cropped to remove the surrounding interface.

This article builds from basic following and hand contact to improvements in turning, hand poses, and network synchronization, guided by debugging and feedback.

1. Design goals and control model

Hand-holding appears to mean simply bringing two players’ hands together, but requires coordinating four systems:

  1. Interaction state: who invites, who accepts, when it starts, and when it ends.
  2. Root movement: the recipient follows the initiator across terrain, turns, and teleports.
  3. Animation: major actions stay aligned, while the recipient’s gait reflects its own actual movement.
  4. Hand IK: arms of different lengths and orientations approach a shared contact point within joint limits.

The results must also agree across initiator, recipient, and observer views. The project uses a single-authority model on the initiator:

  • The initiator owns local movement and calculates the recipient’s follow position, movement animation parameters, and shared IK target.
  • The recipient freezes local movement input and its KCC Motor, consuming the initiator’s results.
  • Observers consume the same paired snapshots and display both players at a common playback time.

Authority here identifies the source of client presentation calculations. The server maintains interaction relationships and business data; clients establish or remove control from room state. Body movement, arm targets, and animation states are managed separately so several systems do not write the same presentation result.

2. Architecture and data flow

2.1 Components and update timing

HoldHandComponent composes three controllers, dispatched externally by PlayerInteractionRuntimeComponent according to room interaction state:

ComponentResponsibility and update timing
HoldHandRuntimeControllerMaintain local interaction, freeze/restore control; calculate or consume poses after KCC updates, drive recipient animation, and broadcast
HoldHandObserverSyncControllerManage observed pairs and sample a snapshot buffer shared by both players each frame
HoldHandIKRuntimeControllerManage skeleton registration, shared contact, IK pauses/weights, and sending/consuming targets
HoldHandIKLateUpdateDriverRun IK in LateUpdate with execution order 10000, after animation and root updates

Movement, remote playback, and bone solving need different update times. Separating them allows personal actions to release hand IK temporarily while preserving the relationship and positional following.

flowchart TB    UI[Intimate interaction entry] -->|Request, accept, cancel| Room[Room PlayerData]    Room --> Dispatch[Interaction state dispatch]    Dispatch --> Runtime[Local hand-holding runtime]    Runtime -->|Calculate after KCC| Pair[Paired poses and recipient animation]    Pair --> Recipient[Recipient snapshot buffer]    Pair --> Observer[Observer snapshot buffer]    Room --> IK[Hand IK controller]    IK -->|Solve in LateUpdate| Targets[Initiator-local IK targets]    Targets --> RemoteIK[Remote LimbIK solving and joint limits]

2.2 A complete interaction sequence

A successful response only confirms protocol handling. Clients drive hand-holding from the IntimacyInteractState actually active in room data:

sequenceDiagram    participant A as Initiator    participant S as Server and room data    participant B as Recipient    participant V as Observer    A->>S: IntimacyInteractReq    S-->>B: PendingIntimacyRequest    B->>S: IntimacyInteractReplyReq(Accept=true)    S-->>A: Initiator、OtherUid、Revision    S-->>B: Recipient、OtherUid、Revision    A->>A: Initialize; start following next frame    B->>B: Freeze Motor; prepare position and animation    A-->>B: Paired poses, SampleTime, Revision    A-->>V: The same paired poses    A-->>B: Recipient animation parameters and IK targets    A-->>V: Animation and IK targets    A->>S: IntimacyInteractCancelReq    S-->>A: Clear interaction state    S-->>B: Clear interaction state

3. Interaction state and lifecycle

3.1 Request and acceptance

Entry points send requests through IntimacyComponent.RequestInteractionAsync, ReplyInteractionAsync, and related interfaces. Before requesting, check the target, shared room, busy states, and restrictions such as transformations. End conflicting personal actions before inviting.

The core request fields are:

Type corresponds to ItemId.IntimacyAction_QianShou, currently 7030001. After server-confirmed acceptance, both players receive states pointing to each other:

PlayerRoleOtherUid
InitiatorInitiatorRecipient UID
RecipientRecipientInitiator UID

Pair validation requires matching roles, type, and partner UIDs. A pose packet’s InteractionRevision must also match the current interaction, preventing late data from another relationship from affecting this one.

3.2 Preparation and active following

State and configuration determine whether the runtime must Begin again. The diagram shows presentation phases; the start frame controls initialization:

stateDiagram-v2    [*] --> Inactive    Inactive --> Initializing: Room hand-holding state becomes active    Initializing --> Following: Initiator reaches the next frame    Following --> Initializing: Identity or configuration changes    Initializing --> Inactive: State becomes invalid    Following --> Inactive: Cancel, leave, or invalid state

The initiator sets m_FollowStartFrame to the current frame plus one and initializes orbit direction and broadcast timers. The recipient immediately freezes movement, disables its Motor, clears animation requests, and switches to the remote animation controller. If the partner entity is loaded, it aligns to the preparation offset and plays the teleport effect.

This one-frame gap distinguishes initialization from continuous driving. IK pairing likewise waits until the frame after first observation before entering the connected phase.

3.3 Exit and room changes

Normal cancellation uses the cancel request and state cleanup. Stop unfreezes control, restores the original Motor-enabled state and Animator, and clears snapshots, drive position, turning state, and cached animation speed. Invalid pairs also release IK.

Before changing rooms, dissolve the relationship; a failed cancellation blocks the change. On success, clear local state before stopping presentation to avoid re-entering hand-holding next frame. The outer dispatcher also stops the local runtime when a partner leaves. Large teleports within the same room are handled by positional following.

4. Positional following and movement smoothing

4.1 Design goals

The recipient should maintain suitable formation while visibly catching up naturally. It must keep up on straight runs, orbit at a controlled speed during stationary turns, use sensible heights on slopes and steps, and arrive promptly after teleportation.

These goals involve horizontal motion, orbital rotation, vertical height, and discontinuous position changes, which need separate calculations and tuning. Network buffering handles remote playback; this section explains the initiator’s authoritative position calculation each frame.

Throughout the diagrams, a red round-headed triangle represents the initiator, and a blue round-headed diamond represents the recipient. The midpoint at each icon’s feet is the character root. Crosses or hollow markers are calculated targets, not actual positions. Each group keeps its scene and scale consistent, labels before/after states as “State 1,” “State 2,” and so on, and places explanations outside the diagram.

4.2 Local offsets and distance-proportional following

Start with a simple design: place a target beside the initiator that rotates with its facing, and let the recipient approach it according to distance. This produces basic formation and following with controls concentrated in offset and catch-up speed.

4.2.1 The active follow target

Start with just two people. The initiator leads; the recipient is led. The red triangle and blue diamond identify them, with foot midpoints indicating positions.

Without follow control, the initiator walks ahead while the recipient stays put:

They drift apart, so first define where the recipient should stand.

Add a formation point. Choose a position beside the initiator, such as slightly behind on the left, and mark it with a cross. The point moves with the initiator. Placing the recipient directly there every frame gives the simplest following:

This preserves formation but makes the recipient feel attached rigidly to the initiator, without a natural catch-up motion. A sudden target change also causes an immediate jump. The next subsection keeps the same point and changes only how the recipient reaches it.

Express formation as a character-relative offset. Lateral and forward/back distances define the point and follow the initiator’s position and facing. FollowOffset describes this: about 0.82 m left and 0.17 m behind creates a slightly staggered side-by-side formation, consistent across facing directions.

Entry also uses PreparationOffset for a one-time alignment; active following uses FollowOffset. Preparation and continuous pursuit serve different purposes:

Object or directionCodePurpose
Initiatorinitiator.RootTransform.positionWorld position for the formation
Character right, forward, and facinginitiator.RootTransform.rotationDefine character axes and rotate local offsets into world space
Lateral and longitudinal formation offsetsFollowOffsetDistance from the character along local X/Z for the horizontal configuration
Preparation offset and positionPreparationOffset, preparation positionAlign once when entering interaction
Formation pointtargetPositionFollow target relative to the root after transforming the offset into world space

4.2.2 A spring model

Let the recipient catch up frame by frame. Instead of directly aligning each frame, advance a small distance from its own position. Farther means faster; nearer means slower, as if a spring connected it to the target.

The spring coefficient sets catch-up strength at a given distance. The blue arrow is this frame’s step, also dependent on elapsed time: at the same speed, a shorter frame produces a smaller step. Each result becomes the next frame’s drive position.

Distance-only speed has two limits: a large gap can produce excessive speed, while a small gap can converge too slowly.

Add minimum and maximum speeds. Small gaps still get sufficient pursuit, while large gaps cannot increase speed without bound:

Limits make pursuit easier to configure, but minimum speed can still produce oversized steps near the target. A basic implementation snaps within a stop radius to finish alignment; section 4.6.1 addresses the resulting fixed-distance discontinuity.

MoveTowards advances using speed and frame duration, stopping at the target when the frame budget reaches it rather than overshooting. The diagrams explain distance and steps, not a scale simulation of the example values below.

Geometric markerCodePurpose
Recipient at the start of pursuitm_DrivenPosition / drivenPositionUse the initiator’s previous calculated result as this frame’s starting point
Remaining distanceVector3.Distance(drivenPosition, targetPosition)Distance to pursue, used to calculate speed
Recipient after advancementnextPositionSave this frame’s result for the next frame
This frame’s stepSpeed and nonnegative elapseSecondsAt equal speed, shorter frames produce less movement; never advance backward

DataHoldHandControl.CalculateFollowSpeed and Vector3.MoveTowards perform this calculation. Example basic-follow parameters are:

ParameterControlExampleMeaning
SpringCoefficientSpring coefficient16Catch-up strength at a given distance
MinFollowSpeedMinimum speed12 m/sMinimum pursuit speed outside the stop radius
MaxFollowSpeedMaximum speed24 m/sLimit pursuit across large gaps
StopRadiusStop radius0.02 mError radius for snapping directly to the target

This spring is not a strict second-order physical spring. It is an engineering model of distance-proportional speed, limits, and bounded movement, without mass or damping parameters, making stable behavior easier for designers to tune.

Crucially, m_DrivenPosition does not read the remote recipient entity’s interpolated position. Packet delay can leave that entity behind; reusing it as the next starting point feeds network jitter back into authoritative calculation and creates an increasingly unstable feedback loop.

4.2.3 Basic behavior and tradeoffs

The recipient can now remain near the initiator and catch up during movement. This has two immediate benefits:

  • Local offsets naturally preserve relative formation with simple rotation and movement logic.
  • A bounded spring avoids teleporting for one snapshot error, with independently tunable speed limits.

Sharp turns, rapidly crossing obstacles, or server corrections inevitably create pursuit lag. (That is not necessarily a drawback: rigid positional motion would not feel like one person leading another.)

Basic following therefore does not require the recipient to be pinned to the target at every moment. Some lag conveys being led. The next improvements concern sharp-turn speed and terrain adaptation, keeping pursuit natural.

4.3 Speed and height problems in playtests

Local offsets and distance-proportional speed preserve formation, but the initiator’s turn rotates the entire offset immediately. A sharp stationary turn sends the target quickly to the other side and can make pursuit feel like being flung around. Simply reducing follow speed also affects ordinary walking and running.

Tuning could not easily satisfy both running and sharp turns. Speed sufficient to keep up with walking/running produced overly fast orbiting. Lower speed softened turns but eventually failed to keep up with runs. Straight pursuit and turning shared one speed constraint; they needed separate handling rather than repeated adjustment of one number.

Further playtesting revealed two related problems: fixed height offsets could bury the recipient in the ground, and stationary turns could leave it in Idle while sliding sideways. Orbit targets, ground height, and animation from actual movement all needed adjustment together.

4.4 Separate horizontal pursuit from orbital rotation

To preserve pursuit while independently tuning turns, I split horizontal following, orbital rotation, and ground height. Distance-proportional following still approaches the target; independent rotation state determines its orbit; ground probing handles height.

First consider an instantly rotated target. Behind-left is relative to the initiator’s facing. If the initiator suddenly turns right and the target immediately adopts that direction, it jumps to the other side:

The spring sees a larger gap and accelerates the recipient. Lowering pursuit speed softens turns but can undermine normal running.

Let the formation point orbit frame by frame too. Keep spring pursuit but change target motion: after the turn, the point gradually moves around the initiator. Each frame updates the target first, then advances the recipient from its previous position.

The black dashed line is the target’s traveled path, and the blue solid line the recipient’s actual path. The blue dashed arrow points toward this frame’s not-yet-reached target:

The model has grown from two independent characters into spring pursuit of a smoothly orbiting target. The recipient still advances in bounded straight steps each frame; many small steps form the actual trajectory.

To distinguish both paths, these flat-ground diagrams use a pursuit coefficient of 8 and speeds of 0.2–0.6 m/s. Rotation smoothing stays at 0.2 s, angular speed at 180°/s, and stop radius at 0.05 m. They follow code update order at 60 fps without networking or collision. Actual resource settings pursue more tightly, so the paths usually lie closer together.

Handle height separately through the ground. Earlier diagrams show level terrain. Pitch or roll can give the rotated offset a vertical component, pulling the recipient off the ground. Keep only the horizontal offset first, placing the target at the initiator’s height; then handle grounding or airborne following:

The blue rotated offset comes from transforming the local offset by the formation-reference rotation. Removing its vertical component gives the red horizontal offset. This reference is specifically for the formation point and smoothly catches up with the initiator’s turn; section 4.6.2 distinguishes it from recipient body facing.

PreparationOffset and FollowOffset use two horizontal components for lateral and longitudinal distances. Preparation places the recipient one meter behind; active following targets about 0.55 m left and 0.22 m behind. The direction is orbit-smoothed, projected horizontally, then given grounded or airborne height. The recipient’s body faces the initiator’s direction.

Movement still begins from the initiator’s stored drive position. Distance selects a speed within limits, the stop region gradually reduces it, and frame duration determines the step. Stop when reaching the target; a zero stop radius omits this extra deceleration.

Distinguish when distance is measured: with grounding allowed, temporarily set target height to drive height, advance using horizontal distance, then probe the ground. Without grounding, pursue using three-dimensional distance including height. Excess-distance teleport checks occur before this height adjustment and always include height difference.

ParameterDiagram labelCurrent resource valuePurpose
SpringCoefficientSpring coefficient40Unclamped growth of speed with distance
MinFollowSpeedMinimum speed2.5 m/sLower bound before stop-region deceleration
MaxFollowSpeedMaximum speed8 m/sUpper pursuit speed
StopRadiusDeceleration radius0.05 mDistance range for continuous deceleration
FollowTeleportDistanceTeleport threshold8 mRebuild the position baseline when 3D distance exceeds it

4.5 KCC integration and modules

KCC drives character movement in the project. The initiator continues ordinary KCC motion. During hand-holding, the recipient disables its local Motor and clears movement, jump, gravity input, and base velocity. Exit restores its saved enabled state.

ModuleResponsibility
HoldHandRuntimeControllerMaintain drive position and calculate following, grounding, and teleportation
HoldHandRotationFollowStateMaintain orbital lag angle and angular velocity
HoldHandGroundSnapDebouncerDebounce grounding-state changes
ControllerSelfPlayer.OnKccUpdateDoneApply hand-holding poses after KCC updates, before camera sampling
DataHoldHandControlCentralize offsets, speed, height, and smoothing parameters

4.6 Movement and smoothing improvements

4.6.1 Continuous deceleration in the stop region

Minimum speed preserves pursuit strength but can still overshoot the desired step near the target. Snapping when close finishes alignment but creates a jump that does not shrink with frame duration.

Add only a deceleration region: once inside, a smaller remaining gap means lower speed, so the final approach also completes frame by frame:

A larger StopRadius starts extra deceleration earlier. Minimum speed applies before this reduction, so actual speed inside can fall below it. Spring coefficient, speed bounds, and radius together determine pursuit and settling. Zero radius omits extra deceleration.

MoveTowards combines speed with frame duration. It reaches the target only when this frame’s step can cover the gap, keeping small-distance movement time-bounded even at high frame rates.

The drive position comes only from the authority’s own calculation, never the already-interpolated remote entity, preventing network jitter from feeding back into pursuit.

4.6.2 Orbital lag and angular speed limits

Section 4.4 separated target orbit from recipient pursuit. One distinction deserves clarification: movement direction and body facing are different. Position pursues the target, while body facing directly follows the initiator, so they can differ during turns:

followRotation determines where the formation point orbits. It is a reference for calculating formation: when the initiator has already turned but this reference is still catching up, the point moves gradually around it. It does not directly set recipient body rotation.

Gradual turning alone is insufficient; sharp turns still need response control. Rotation smoothing shapes catch-up, and maximum angular speed caps each frame’s actual turn. Current RotationFollowSmoothTime is 0.2 s and MaxRotationFollowSpeed is 180°/s.

Each frame follows this order:

  1. Read this frame’s initiator yaw change and accumulate the unconsumed angle.
  2. Consume it with SmoothDamp, then bound the actual angle by frame duration to obtain formation-reference rotation.
  3. Transform FollowOffset with that reference to produce this frame’s formation point.
  4. Measure from the stored drive position to the target, determine the step from distance-proportional speed, limits, and stop-region deceleration, then call MoveTowards.
  5. Correct height according to grounding conditions and apply recipient position; use initiator rotation directly for body facing.
ObjectCodePurpose
Initiator body facinginitiatorRotation and its yawDesired facing for this frame
Formation-reference rotationResult of HoldHandRotationFollowState.Update, namely followRotationDetermine where the target orbits
This frame’s formation pointtargetPositionPursuit target calculated from reference rotation and offset
Current recipient positionm_DrivenPositionStarting point for this frame’s advancement
Black target trajectoryEach frame’s targetPositionSubject to rotation smoothing and angular limits
Blue recipient trajectoryEach frame’s nextPositionPursue the point frame by frame, bounded by movement speed and stop-region deceleration

For comparison, simulating the same stationary 90° right turn at 60 fps with current resource settings gives a maximum target–recipient gap of about 6 mm. Section 4.4 deliberately slows pursuit to clarify update order. Actual gaps depend on the balance of linear pursuit and angular limits.

m_AngularVelocity stores smoothing velocity; m_LagAngle stores unconsumed angle. Continuous turning retains orbit direction without accumulating full revolutions to catch up. After about 0.05 s without turning, it settles by the nearest route. Reversal also limits residual angular velocity pushing the target away. Zero smoothing time or maximum orbit speed uses initiator facing directly.

This separates linear pursuit speed from target orbit speed. Running retains enough catch-up ability while turning moves the target at a controlled angular speed. Visible lag depends on the relative constraints during the current action.

4.6.3 Grounding debounce and landing-height limits

The simplest height handling reuses initiator height. On slopes, the ground beneath each player differs, leaving the recipient floating or buried.

Cast downward from above the recipient and correct its height to the hit ground, while keeping spring-controlled horizontal motion:

This handles ordinary slopes, but edges can repeatedly change grounded state, and rays can hit high platforms or deep ground. Add state debounce and landing-height limits separately.

Recipient grounding is allowed when the initiator is stably grounded, KCC permits snapping, and the height difference is within limits. Advance horizontally first, then probe downward.

At step edges, grounding may alternate. HoldHandGroundSnapDebouncer requires a candidate state to persist before switching. Current debounce is 2 s and maximum height difference 0.5 m. Exceeding that difference immediately disables grounding without waiting.

After a ray hit, also check its height relative to the initiator. This hard limit prevents already-enabled grounding from snapping the recipient to a high platform or deep surface.

On the left, initiator and recipient markers are actual positions. The ray starts above the recipient; the ground candidate, landing-height difference, and blue height boundary determine acceptance. On the right, the red line is candidate grounding, blue is active snapping, and debounce duration marks required persistence. Side-view geometry is not drawn to meter scale.

Geometric markerCodePurpose
Probe elevationRecipientGroundProbeHeightCast from 10 m above the position being projected
Ray lengthRecipientGroundProbeDistanceProbe at most 100 m downward from the ray origin
Allowed and actual landing-height differencesGroundSnapMaxHeightDifference, measured differenceA hit may differ from initiator height by at most 0.5 m; a ray hit alone does not pass this limit
Debounce durationGroundSnapDebounceDurationRequired candidate persistence before switching; currently 2 s
Grounding candidateStable grounding with SnappingPrevented falseOnly stable ground eligible for snapping can request grounding
Ground-snapping stateuseGroundSnappingChoose horizontal advance plus projection or full 3D pursuit

Rays use the recipient’s stable-ground layer configuration, fall back to the map layer when invalid, and ignore triggers. Debounce retains grounding mode, but excessive height difference disables it immediately, and each landing must independently pass the height check.

4.6.4 Align KCC and camera sampling phases

If following reads physics positions while the camera later reads interpolated display positions, the body and camera use different phases in one frame. Align the order: update character display positions, calculate following, then sample the camera.

Authoritative calculation and recipient application both happen in OnKccUpdateDone, using KCC-interpolated display positions before camera sampling. Body, target, and camera then share a phase, avoiding jitter from mixing fixed-step motion with render frames.

On the initiator’s client, the recipient entity directly applies per-frame results, avoiding stacked local-follow and network-playback smoothing.

4.6.5 Reset smoothing after teleportation

Spring pursuit suits ordinary movement, but teleportation can suddenly separate the pair too far for slow catch-up. Add a threshold: beyond it, align directly to the new formation and restart following there.

The dashed circle is a cross-section of the 3D threshold sphere. Teleport threshold is FollowTeleportDistance; pursuit distance is the 3D gap from drive position to target. The height marker emphasizes vertical displacement. Exactly reaching the threshold still uses ordinary following.

When drive-to-target distance exceeds 8 m, use the new formation under the initiator’s current facing, reset orbital angle, grounding debounce, and recipient animation speed, and immediately broadcast a Teleported result.

Teleportation is discontinuous movement. Clearing smoothing caches prevents drifting along the old direction or slowly crossing a large gap. The networking section describes corresponding remote-buffer resets.

4.7 Connecting actions during integration

After adding rotation solving, I used demonstrations and actual play with designers to verify orbit behavior, then checked walking, running, and stationary turns. The focus was whether body facing and gait connected naturally once target motion became steadier.

Orbiting also turns the recipient’s body. Keeping Idle would make it slide while standing. Body facing therefore still follows the initiator, while movement animation uses the recipient’s own actual velocity, described in section 5.

4.8 Comparing both follow designs

Both use the initiator as the calculation source and retain a separate drive position for the recipient. They differ mainly in target generation, speed allocation, near-target behavior, and terrain handling.

Design pointLocal offset and proportional pursuitSeparate orbit and horizontal pursuit
Target turningOffset rotates directly with initiator facingSmooth offset direction separately and bound angular speed
Speed tuningOne pursuit configuration affects straight motion and orbitingConfigure linear pursuit and angular orbit speed separately
Near targetSnap inside the stop radiusContinuously decelerate with time-bounded displacement
HeightFull 3D root-transformed offsetSeparate horizontal offset and height; debounce grounding and limit landing height
