Large changesPursue at configured speedAlign beyond a threshold and reset motion/smoothing
Implementation costFew states; easy basic followingMaintain angular velocity, grounding state, and reset timing

Local offsets and proportional speed already express paired following. When natural turns, complex terrain, and stable frame-to-frame behavior matter, separating constraints provides clearer tuning control.

5. Animation synchronization and parameter smoothing

5.1 Design goals

Both players should share major action semantics—walking, jumping, gliding—while recipient gait matches its own displacement. It may orbit while the initiator turns in place or keep catching up after the initiator stops.

The animation system must reserve control for holding, harvesting, one-handed operations, and personal actions, preventing hand-holding mirroring from overwriting them.

5.2 Design and principles

The initiator supplies snapshots of mirrorable layers and derives recipient velocity from its solved horizontal displacement each frame. Transforming velocity into initiator-root local coordinates produces SpeedPerc_XZ, SpeedPerc_LocalX, and SpeedPerc_LocalZ for the recipient’s movement blend tree.

Ordinary grounded Move/Idle uses recipient speed, while jumping and gliding retain initiator action states. Broadcasts carry recipient-specific snapshots; remote clients consume them directly so all three views use the same speed source.

5.3 Animator integration and modules

ModuleResponsibility
HoldHandRuntimeControllerGenerate and smooth recipient velocity once per frame; maintain periodic refreshes
ControllerSelfPlayer.HoldHandCopy mirrorable snapshots and write recipient movement parameters
HoldHandStateUtilityDetermine mirrorable layers, recipient operation layers, and whether the right hand is occupied
Recipient animation driverConsume authoritative states and switch between remote and personal-action controllers

The recipient normally uses OtherPlayerAnimatorController; local movement input does not decide ordinary gait. Personal actions validate action IDs and load Clips, while holding and harvesting use their own logic.

5.4 Animation smoothing and compatibility

5.4.1 Advance velocity filtering only once

Ground-height changes must not count as running. Remove displacement’s Y component, cap velocity at MaxFollowSpeed, then apply exponential smoothing with AnimationVelocitySmoothTime = 0.1 s:

\[\alpha=1-e^{-\Delta t/\tau},\qquad\bar v_{next}=\operatorname{Lerp}(\bar v,v_{raw},\alpha)\]

Update this velocity only once after the initiator solves movement each frame. Animation layers and broadcasts only read it, so layer count and send frequency do not alter filtering speed. This suppresses gait jitter from SpeedPerc fluctuations.

5.4.2 Start/stop hysteresis and teleport reset

Start and stop thresholds are 0.1 m/s and 0.05 m/s. Stopping checks both raw and smoothed velocity to reduce toggling near rest. Teleportation clears velocity and movement flags so a large displacement is not interpreted as fast running.

The base layer refreshes at an independent interval, allowing recipient pursuit or orbit animation to keep updating even while the initiator is idle.

5.4.3 Yield to operation layers and personal actions

ShouldMirrorAnimationLayer excludes recipient upper-body, one-hand, two-hand, Base_1, and personal-action display layers, preserving their own driving sources.

Supported personal actions increment an entry counter, pause hand-holding IK and associated music, and restore the local Animator controller when needed. When the final personal action ends, restore the hand-holding controller and held-item presentation. An operation occupying the recipient’s right hand temporarily zeros that side’s IK weight so the operation animation controls the arm.

6. Hand IK

6.1 Design goals

Hand IK brings the initiator’s left hand and recipient’s right hand together while maintaining natural shoulders, elbows, and wrists. Different arm lengths, attachment offsets, and body positions require a shared target inside both reach ranges, followed by joint-constrained bone results.

During running, jumping, and turning, contact should move stably with the pair. Gliding or personal actions that occupy the arms must release and restore it smoothly. IK changes arm presentation only; movement owns root positions.

IK diagrams retain red initiator and blue recipient icons. Each shows both participating chains: six circular nodes in total. Red and blue shoulder → elbow → wrist chains each map to LimbIK’s bone1 → bone2 → bone3. Crosses mark logical points such as palms and contact targets; dashed reference chains add no actual nodes.

These are 2D geometric explanations. Successive states preserve upper-arm and forearm lengths to show changing inputs, targets, and constraints; proportions and poses are not real-device parameter calibration.

6.2 Shared contact and reachability

Basic hand contact starts by making two arms approach the same point. Derive a preferred point from both hand Poses, constrain it by their reach ranges, and solve through Final IK LimbIK. Connection state and weight transitions complete basic hand-holding.

6.2.1 Derive a shared Pose from two contact Poses

First consider two arms and one common target. Each arm has shoulder, elbow, and wrist nodes; temporarily treat the wrist endpoint as contact. Keep shoulders fixed and adjust elbows/wrists toward one target.

Adjusting joints backward from a specified endpoint target is inverse kinematics, or IK. This produces basic contact but does not yet establish whether both arms can reach; reachability comes next.

Place both contact Poses in world space. Average their positions and use Quaternion.Slerp at 0.5 for rotation. This result, before reach constraints, smoothing, and final offsets, is the preferred Pose. Code stores it as preferredContact before constraints to reveal how later processing changes it.

Currently these inputs come from stable references captured and reconstructed in section 6.4.1, rather than freshly animated hand Poses each frame. Both sides use one contact position, adding InitiatorContactRotationOffset and RecipientContactRotationOffset separately for grip orientation.

This establishes a shared target. LimbIK’s wrist targets must still be derived from palm attachments, as explained in section 6.5.3.

6.2.2 Approximate two-segment arms with reach spheres

Both chains now pursue a common point. Move that point farther away: elbows can extend, but hands cannot stretch indefinitely because upper-arm and forearm lengths are fixed.

Add only the two fixed bone lengths, then approximate their coverage with reach spheres. The diagrams show cross-sections comparing bent and extended states:

The simplest radius sums upper-arm and forearm lengths. Bending brings the hand closer; extension reaches farther, without changing length or coverage. A palm attachment offset can shift the sphere center, so the diagram separates it from the shoulder. Section 6.4.2 describes another approach that reserves reach margin.

With both spheres, TryConstrainSharedContact limits the preferred point to shared space. Spheres describe reach; elbow bending direction and angular joint limits need separate handling.

6.2.3 Sphere-intersection constraints

Individual reach still does not guarantee contact: distant players can have disjoint ranges. First consider them approaching until their ranges intersect:

Red and blue dashed circles are reach-sphere cross-sections. Once an intersection exists, bring an external target back into shared reach. Without one, a compromise remains and simultaneous contact cannot be guaranteed.

The implementation selects candidates in this order:

  1. Use the preferred point directly if it lies inside both spheres.
  2. For disjoint spheres, choose a compromise along the center line according to both reach capacities and set HasSharedReach false.
  3. For intersecting spheres with an external preferred point, test projections onto individual spheres; choose the nearest candidate satisfying both ranges.
  4. If neither projection works, use the spheres’ intersection circle to project and constrain the preferred point to the shared region.

The intersection circle defines the common boundary; its radius also depends on attachment margins. This establishes geometric reachability, while elbow direction and joint rotation require additional limits.

6.2.4 Smoothing, connection state, and weights

Even with shared reach, target changes and connection switches can look abrupt. Smooth the shared target frame by frame, then handle connection boundaries and arm influence.

Smooth contact in initiator-root local space using Vector3.SmoothDamp, currently with ContactPositionSmoothTime = 0.01 s. If a shared range exists, constrain the smoothed point back into it to avoid crossing boundaries during transition. Section 6.6.2 covers the full local-space process.

A newly observed pair first passes a preparation frame. From the next frame, it connects while valid and unpaused. Gliding and personal actions disconnect IK; it resumes when every pause reason disappears.

Current UpdateConnection does not use player distance. HasSharedReach separately records simultaneous reach and does not directly end the interaction or IK connection.

Connection selects a target weight of 1 or 0. Actual weight approaches it gradually instead of making the whole arm jump instantly:

These diagrams show transition endpoints; intermediate weights advance each frame. Connection affects IK without clearing room interaction state. Maximum position and rotation weights are both 1, with 0.3 s fade-in and fade-out. Position weight controls pursuit by the chain; rotation weight controls wrist orientation. Targets go to LimbIK.solver each frame before manual solving.

6.2.5 Basic behavior and tradeoffs

Shared targets, reach constraints, and weight transitions already connect both hands. Their advantages are:

  • One contact point gives both hands a stable visual grip location, rather than independent targets.
  • Sphere intersections are inexpensive, have clear boundaries, and explicitly handle unequal arm lengths.
  • Preparation, pause state, and fading support continuous entry, release, and recovery.
  • Initiator computation and broadcasting keep results consistent without requiring recipients and observers to repeat full reachability logic.
  • Final IK LimbIK reuses existing skeletons and bend configurations at low integration cost.

This is suitable for establishing basic contact before tuning offsets and weights through playtests. Geometric reachability does not eliminate the need to inspect arm poses in motion.

6.3 Hand-pose problems during movement

Spheres express reachability, not elbow preferences, shoulder limits, colliders, or clothing constraints. Some poses invert elbows or intersect bodies. Disjoint spheres still only yield a compromise, and changing contact, bone animation, and root motion together can introduce hand swing into solving.

Aligning hands while stationary proved insufficient. Contact could fold awkwardly, movement showed stutter and hand swing, wrists sometimes bent unnaturally, and arms pulled upward during large-jump descent. Animation’s influence on solving needed control beyond contact alignment.

One clear reproduction was running into a collision: IK stayed misplaced until disconnecting and reconnecting. Hands also looked unnatural after small and large jumps. Improvements focused on stable contact/bone references that current animation could not continually redefine, plus separate shoulder, elbow, and wrist limits.

Reference-pose stability reproduction: abnormal contact on the left, re-established connection on the right.

6.4 Stable references and constrained shared targets

To preserve contact during running, jumping, and pause recovery, I retained shared targets and sphere constraints but fixed inputs to stable reference poses. Targets change only with the pair’s relative relationship; bone results receive separate joint limits and smoothing.

6.4.1 The initiator computes shared contact

Reading current animated hand contact every frame can carry arm swing or one bad pose into later targets. Instead, capture both hands’ character-relative positions and rotations when hand-holding is established.

This is local space: the reference records where the hand is relative to its character, not an absolute map position. Whole-character movement carries it along; animated wrists can swing without redefining it:

When both attachments and chains first become usable, save each contact Pose in its own root’s local space. Each frame reconstruct them from current roots, average position and rotation into the preferred Pose, then apply reach constraints, local smoothing, and final offsets. Current animation never redefines the baseline.

These diagrams show reference reading; solid chains are animation poses before IK. preferredContact is the newly formed, unprocessed preferred Pose. Reach constraints change its position but retain the intermediate rotation. Local smoothing, re-constraint, and ContactPositionOffset follow, producing shared position and independent rotations. The initiator performs the full calculation; remote clients consume local targets.

6.4.2 Intersecting both reach spheres

Using complete arm lengths can still push wrists to full extension. Palm attachments lie beyond the wrist, and orientation/contact-distance changes need margin.

Keep sphere centers at shoulders and reserve palm offsets from their radii; reserve extra contact distance when needed. Each diagram changes only one margin:

Centers use shoulders. Radius sums both bone lengths minus the palm attachment offset and absolute PalmContactDistance, leaving extension margin for wrist rotation and spacing. A nonpositive remaining radius cannot form a valid reach sphere.

The diagrams vary contact spacing to explain it; the current resource’s PalmContactDistance is zero. Intersection uses section 6.2.3’s candidates and projections. Without an intersection, keep trying with a compromise target; joint limits still protect the final arms.

6.4.3 Pair validity and connection state

IK accepts only mutually linked, same-type states with downloaded Avatars and ready skeletons. Connection starts after the first-observation preparation frame when no pause reason remains.

Gliding and personal actions use a set of pause reasons; recovery waits until all are cleared. HasSharedReach describes geometry, not whether interaction or IK disconnects. Invalid skeletons, weather transformations, and recipient right-hand operations have separate release or yield logic.

6.5 Applying Final IK and dividing modules

6.5.1 Solve each arm with LimbIK

The project uses Final IK (namespace RootMotion.FinalIK). LimbIK solves one limb. Each character prepares left and right arm solvers; hand-holding uses the initiator’s left and recipient’s right.

LimbIK uses IKSolverLimb, derived from the law-of-cosines analytic IKSolverTrigonometric. Its three-node upper-arm, forearm, and wrist chain has two bone lengths. Given an endpoint and bend plane, it computes the pose and exposes endpoint rotation and weights.

IKSolverLimb.BendModifier.Arm supplies an arm-suitable bend plane. Project modules own shared targets, network authority, pause state, and three-axis limits; the plugin solves the chain itself.

6.5.2 Bind chains and update manually

EntityBaseHead.InitializeHoldHandIK uses G_LweaponTransform and G_RweaponTransform as contact attachments. Traversing upward yields wrist, forearm, and upper arm; validation precedes solver creation. Core setup is:

Disable LimbIK’s automatic component update, set targets with SetIKPosition and SetIKRotation, then manually call limb.solver.Update() at the controlled phase. This solves after animation and applies limits afterward, avoiding independently scheduled updates.

fixTransforms = false gives project code control of reference-pose restoration; target = null means writing target Poses directly without a target Transform. An invalid attachment, chain, or LimbIK prevents valid registration.

6.5.3 Convert palm targets into wrist targets

Earlier contact was simplified to one endpoint. In the plugin, the endpoint is the wrist, but gameplay aligns palms. Treating palm contact as a wrist target ignores the attachment offset.

Keep the palm target fixed and change grip orientation: as the offset rotates, the wrist must move to keep the palm on target.

First cancel the attachment’s wrist-local rotation to derive wrist orientation. Scale the local attachment position by character scale, rotate it into world space with that orientation, and subtract it from the palm target to obtain the wrist target.

The diagram enlarges offsets for clarity. ContactTargetToHandTarget takes the contact Pose, contact.localRotation, contact.localPosition, and wrist lossyScale. Only the derived wrist Pose goes into LimbIK. PalmContactDistance is applied beforehand.

6.5.4 Project/plugin boundaries

ModuleResponsibility
HoldHandIKRuntimeControllerEnumerate valid pairs, calculate shared contact, manage weights/pauses, and send or consume authoritative targets
HoldHandIKPairStateStore reference contact Poses, position smoothing, network sequences, and remote targets
EntityBaseHead.HoldHandIKRegister skeletons, bind LimbIK, convert palm targets, maintain arm references, and solve
Final IK LimbIK / IKSolverLimbSolve a three-node arm from wrist targets and bend mode
HoldHandArmRotationLimitsSmooth and limit shoulder, elbow, and wrist rotations across three axes; prevent reverse elbow bending
HoldHandIKLateUpdateDriverCoordinate each frame’s IK update phase
DataHoldHandControlConfigure contact offsets, smoothing, weights, and joint ranges

6.6 IK stability and smoothing improvements

6.6.1 Fix reference poses to isolate animation disturbance

Running swings and jumps continually change bones. Extracting a new baseline every frame changes targets and limit references, potentially carrying an abnormal pose into the next solve.

Save local contact Poses per pair and arm reference rotations at the first valid solve separately. Contact follows roots; chains solve from stable references. Temporary pauses such as gliding retain them. Pair rebuilding or invalid skeletons reset them through lifecycle handling.

6.6.2 Smooth contact in character-local space

Stable references reduce arm-swing disturbance, but relative motion can still make shared contact jump. World-space smoothing would also make targets trail whole-character movement and jumps.

Smooth only changes relative to the initiator: overall displacement carries the target immediately, while relative changes converge gradually.

Apply SmoothDamp in initiator-root local space with 0.01 s smoothing, then transform back to world space. Only relative changes are smoothed; whole-character movement and jumps carry the target immediately, avoiding world-space lag.

The diagram initially shows only local target and smoothed contact. Reach constraints and configured offsets add two steps:

With shared reach, project the smoothed result back into that region. Then add root-rotated ContactPositionOffset, currently (-0.04, -0.31, -0.01). Do not write the offset into the smoothing cache, preventing accumulation or later smoothing from overwriting it. It may move the target outside reach, so tune it alongside bone limits.

Remote IK targets are also smoothed in initiator-local space and reconstructed using the locally displayed root. Section 7 explains their consumption.

6.6.3 Three-axis limits and preventing reverse elbow bending

Shared contact determines where hands go, and reach determines whether they can arrive. Neither guarantees natural joints. Add separate shoulder, elbow, and wrist ranges and prevent reverse bending: solve IK first, then constrain final bones.

HoldHandArmRotationLimits supplies yaw, pitch, and roll ranges separately. Upper arms reference the character, elbows the upper arm, and wrists the forearm. Bone axes are calibrated at initialization; reference frames follow character or parent-bone rotation at runtime.

Shoulder, elbow, and wrist limit arcs mark constraint locations. The implementation limits all three axes; the 2D diagram explains order rather than measuring actual resource angles.

Joint configuration entry points and reference frames; actual values are listed below.

JointYaw rangePitch rangeRoll rangeRotation smoothing
Upper arm-45° to 80°-90° to 10°-45° to 45°0.03 s
Elbow0° to 145°-5° to 5°-80° to 80°0.03 s
Wrist-30° to 20°-45° to 45°-5° to 5°0.03 s

The elbow must satisfy both angular ranges and the normal-flexion half-space. Calculate them together so limiting angles and then preventing reversal do not overwrite each other. An infeasible intersection must not be solved by reverse bending.

6.6.4 Joint rotation smoothing and solve order

Each joint smooths rotation in its own stable frame, currently over 0.03 s. This softens small solver jumps while immediately passing character turns and parent-bone rotations to the arm.

After smoothing, apply hard three-axis limits and cache the constrained rotation, preventing the filter from accumulating error beyond limits. One arm update follows:

  1. Save the animated pose, restore stable references, and solve the complete IK pose with LimbIK.
  2. Apply the overall maximum rotation from the reference pose, then blend with animation using position/rotation weights.
  3. Recompute palm offsets from the blended wrist orientation and run LimbIK to correct contact.
  4. Smooth and constrain shoulders, elbows, and wrists, including elbow-reversal protection, producing this frame’s bones.

Do not run IK again after the final limits. When contact precision conflicts with joint ranges, prioritize joint constraints and allow a small palm gap.

6.6.5 Weight transitions and yielding to operations

Connecting and disconnecting alone do not cover personal actions. An operation can temporarily occupy one arm while the relationship remains active; simultaneous bone writers would overwrite each other.

Add pause/recovery: let animation control arms during pauses, retain this interaction’s references, and gradually restore weight toward those same references afterward.

Connection advances weights through MoveTowards, with 0.3 s fade-in/out and maximum position/rotation weights of 1. Weighted animation/IK blending gives continuous entry, pause, and recovery.

A set of pause reasons prevents one system’s release from overriding another’s occupation. A recipient operation using the right hand temporarily zeros that side’s position and rotation weights. Weather transformations or missing skeletons release IK through their own paths.

6.7 Pose adjustments and retesting

Fixing solve references to entry bone poses improved hand swing during movement. Retests with designers continued examining small lateral shakes, jumps, and collision recovery rather than judging only stationary or straight movement.

Remaining elbow poses and standing slides were handled separately: joint limits and smoothing own bone presentation; actual-speed-driven animation owns gait. Each change corresponds to a specific experience problem.

6.8 Comparing both hand-solving approaches

Both let the initiator determine shared contact and use LimbIK for local chain solving. Additional handling concerns reference poses, target smoothing, and bone constraints.

Design pointShared contact and reach constraintsStable references and joint constraints
Target referencePreferred contact from current hand PosesSave root-local reference Poses and reconstruct from roots
Solve starting poseCurrent animated poseFixed arm reference rotations, then animation blending
ReachArm-length spheres adjusted for attachmentsShoulder-centered spheres reserving palm/contact-distance margins
Contact smoothingWorld-space target smoothingInitiator-local relative smoothing with immediate overall motion
Pose limitsLimbIK bend mode and reach regionSeparate shoulder/elbow/wrist smoothing and limits plus elbow protection
Connection and pausesPreparation frame and weighted entry/releaseExplicit pause reasons; retain references during temporary release
Presentation tradeoffSimpler basic contactMore controlled moving poses; limits can leave small palm gaps
CostManage contact, reach, and weightsAlso manage references, joint frames, smoothing caches, and solve order

Shared contact determines where hands meet; stable references and limits control how arms get there. Body proportions, clothing, and body collisions still require dedicated handling rather than simply increasing IK weight.

7. Network synchronization and playback smoothing

7.1 Design goals

Networking must present the initiator’s paired results stably to recipients and observers, balancing latency against arrival jitter that causes body stutter, stretched player spacing, and jumping hand targets.

Position, animation, and IK change at different rates. Tune their streams independently; they share interaction identity and authority but retain their own consumption and smoothing.

7.2 Design and data model

The initiator sends paired poses, animation snapshots, and IK targets through NetworkServiceComponent. Paired-pose fields include:

FieldPurpose
Both UIDs and interaction typeIdentify the pair and validate room state
Both positions and rotationsTwo root Poses from the same sample
SampleTimeInitiator’s monotonic sample time for ordering and velocity estimates
InteractionRevisionCheck that the snapshot belongs to this interaction
TeleportedClear old trajectories and rebuild the buffer baseline

SampleTime compares only differences from one sender and requires no client clock synchronization. Each recipient or observer maintains its own playback time and samples both poses from one paired buffer.

Independent IK broadcasts carry two local target Poses, Sequence, BlendWeight, Connected, and HasSharedReach. Animation carries initiator-generated recipient movement parameters so remote clients need not infer gait from network displacement.

7.3 Synchronization modules

ModuleResponsibility
NetworkServiceComponent.HoldHandOrganize and send paired-pose and IK broadcasts
BroadcastHoldHandTransformUpdateHandlerValidate pairing, sample time, and revision, then dispatch poses
HoldHandPairSnapshotRepresent both poses at one sample time
HoldHandSnapshotBufferStore the timeline, interpolate, extrapolate within limits, and decay prediction error
HoldHandRuntimeControllerConsume the local recipient buffer and apply both poses together
HoldHandObserverSyncControllerManage observer pairs and apply buffered poses to both entities
HoldHandIKRuntimeController / HoldHandIKPairStateValidate IK sequences and smooth/reconstruct remote local targets

7.4 Networking and smoothing improvements

7.4.1 Share one sample time for both players

First consider displaying each received position immediately. Messages are discrete; without updates between them, the view pauses and jumps when the next arrives:

Fill intermediate states between adjacent positions. Save previous and next positions and display intermediate values each frame: interpolation. Knowing the next position requires delayed playback, adding a little display latency:

Give both players the same playback time. Independent interpolation can still stretch their spacing through different progress. Put poses from one calculation in a paired snapshot and sample both from one timeline.

Sample time records when the initiator captured positions, arrival time when the packet reached this client, and playback cursor which instant is displayed. Both players share that cursor:

HoldHandSnapshotBuffer retains at most 64 paired snapshots. Between samples, positions interpolate linearly and rotations spherically. Both players always use one playback time, preventing independent trajectory errors from accumulating into arm separation.

Three timelines show sender sampling, local arrival, and buffered playback. Arrivals may be uneven, but the cursor advances continuously and both players sample the same instant. Bottom icons represent sampled results, not map formation. Motion speed and interpolation progress use sender time.

ViewPlaybackInterpolation delayMaximum extrapolation
Local initiatorApply authoritative per-frame results directlyNo network bufferUnneeded
Local recipientApply both poses at one time after KCC update0.06 s0.03 s
ObserverPair controller samples/applies both each frame0.09 s0.1 s

Longer buffering absorbs more jitter but adds latency. Recipients and observers therefore have separate delays and extrapolation limits.

7.4.2 Continuous playback time and small speed corrections

Playback advances using continuous local time while targeting a delay behind the latest sample. When buffer depth deviates by more than one position interval, about ±5% playback-speed correction reduces drift, instead of repositioning on every packet.

Even several packets in one frame cannot repeatedly jump playback progress. After long main-thread stalls or excessive lag, realign time to the latest sample minus configured delay and clear corrections.

7.4.3 Bounded extrapolation and prediction-error decay

During packet gaps, estimate velocity from the last two sender sample times and advance only for the configured duration. Extrapolate horizontally at at most 20 m/s; hold latest height and rotation to avoid amplifying ground snaps or guessing turns.

When a new sample corrects the predicted trajectory, record prediction differences at the same playback time and exponentially decay position/rotation error each frame. Correction takes max(0.05 s, interpolation delay), preserving continuity on arrival while returning gradually to authority.

Explicit teleportation, large jumps, or sample gaps beyond resynchronization clear old trajectories and errors and rebuild the baseline. The current gap threshold is 1 s. If no sample arrives by the extrapolation limit, prediction stops.

7.4.4 Tune the three streams independently

DataHoldHandControl centralizes synchronization parameters. Current periodic settings are:

StreamIntervalContent and strategy
Paired poses0.1 s, about 10 HzBoth roots, sample time, revision, and teleport flag
Recipient base-layer refresh0.2 s, about 5 HzContinuously update grounded movement parameters; ordinary animation requests may also trigger sends
IK targets0.2 s, about 5 HzBoth local targets, weights, and connection state; smooth each frame remotely

Separate rates balance bandwidth, latency, and precision by responsibility. Teleports trigger immediate pose and animation broadcasts; recipient reporting reuses ordinary player mechanisms. These are periodic settings, not guaranteed arrival intervals.

7.4.5 Reject stale data and duplicate driving

Pose receivers validate mutual linkage, type, sample time, and InteractionRevision; buffers reject non-increasing sample times. IK compares wrap-aware Sequence values to reject duplicates and out-of-order targets.

Ordinary player packets can update caches but cannot override active paired-pose control. Recipients apply both sampled poses together, and initiators drive their local recipient entities directly, avoiding additional smoothing of the same trajectory.

Poses without sample times use target smoothing: recipients consume targets through SmoothDamp and use relative anchors for partners; observers smooth both targets separately. Valid SampleTime selects the timeline buffer described here.

7.4.6 Synchronize and reconstruct local IK targets

Sending a world-space grip directly can leave hands at the last received point while interpolated bodies move ahead. Misaligned update timing makes hands appear to trail behind.

Instead, record position and rotation relative to the initiator. Remote clients smooth relative changes, then reconstruct targets using currently displayed character roots:

The initiator sends root-relative IK positions and rotations. Remote clients smooth locally, reconstruct world targets using displayed roots, and pass them to both LimbIK solvers.

The diagrams show translation; rotation uses the same root transformation. Remote target/weight smoothing takes half the IK interval with a 0.01 s minimum, currently 0.1 s. Overall root movement passes directly to targets; filters handle relative pose changes.

Remote clients run their own LimbIK and joint limits, not shared-sphere solving. Arms are released before the first IK packet. A valid pair receiving no further packets keeps consuming the last target. There is currently no independent IK timeout; pose extrapolation limits do not provide that protection.

7.5 Retesting observer views

After improving third-party stutter, designers and I retested on the previously problematic devices and confirmed better movement continuity for observers.

The question was whether observers continuously see both players moving together. Local authoritative position and arm calculations must be stable, while remote snapshot playback must tolerate arrival jitter to convey the same following experience.

8. Runtime boundaries and tuning relationships

8.1 Exceptions and fallback behavior

SituationHandling
Both states have not arrivedLocal initialization can start; complete-pair receive validation and IK wait for mutual linkage
Partner entity or Avatar not loadedDefer relevant movement and release IK until ready
Out-of-order poses or another interactionReject by sample time and revision
Brief pose-packet gapsBounded horizontal extrapolation, then stop prediction
Teleport, large jump, or long sample interruptionClear trajectories/corrections and rebuild playback
Ground ray hits an excessive-height surfaceRetain pre-projection position without crossing height limits
Shared contact unreachableKeep solving a compromise target with hard joint protection
Gliding or supported personal actionsPause relevant IK and preserve stable references for recovery
Recipient right-hand operationYield that side’s IK to operation animation
Partner leaves or room changesStop hand-holding and clear state

Ray grounding handles height only, without wall avoidance or complete pathfinding. Joint limits do not implement body/clothing collision constraints. These boundaries define suitable gameplay and acceptable palm gaps or pose changes during debugging.

8.2 What each smoothing mechanism controls

Smoothing or constraintTargetTuning relationship
Proportional speed and stop-region decelerationAuthoritative recipient positionPursuit speed versus near-target stability
Orbital rotation smoothing and limitsFormation offset directionSharp-turn behavior versus orbit lag
Grounding debounce and landing-height limitsGround-follow state and heightStep-edge stability versus switching speed
Velocity filtering and start/stop thresholdsRecipient animation parametersStable gait versus start/stop response
Local contact smoothingShared IK targetRelative hand jitter versus contact response
Joint smoothing and hard limitsShoulder, elbow, and wrist bonesNatural poses versus palm precision
Snapshot interpolation, bounded extrapolation, and error decayRemote paired posesJitter tolerance versus display latency
Remote local IK smoothingReceived hand targets and weightsSend rate versus visual continuity

These mechanisms operate on different data and reference frames. First locate whether jitter originates in authoritative motion, animation parameters, bone solving, or remote playback, then tune that layer. Stacked smoothing should not conceal update-order or control-ownership conflicts.

entry.title: The Evolution of Unity-Autorun-Tool (2026)
entry.content:
At the end of 2024, I built a small Unity auto-clicking tool. Every time I entered the game, I had to wait for the scene to load, then click through the connection, login, and entry buttons. This took about half a minute. The actions were simple, but I had to watch the whole process.

The tool later experimented with UI navigation graphs. Version 0.3.4 now uses compiled C# business scripts: an AI reads the host project’s sources and runtime evidence, prepares a flow with explicit starting conditions and assertions, and lets Unity compile and execute it. For repeated self-tests, I run an existing matching script.

The screenshots in this revision show version 0.3.4 running in an isolated Unity demonstration project. They show actual tool behavior and demo configuration, without a production host project’s business data.

From fixed clicks to business scripts

The first version saved a sequence of button operations and waits. It did not shorten the game’s loading time; it removed the need to sit through several repeated clicks. Navigation graphs later helped organize shared entry paths, but a connection between two views was never enough on its own. An entry might depend on player state or asynchronous loading, and different starting states could require different actions to reach the same destination.

Those conditions now live in compiled business scripts. The old navigation graph, graph routing, and manual XML navigation entry points have been retired. Existing host data is not silently converted or deleted; the workflow below uses C# scripts.

Describe one complete self-test

Before writing a script, the AI inspects the host’s sources, Prefabs, and actual runtime state. The tool core provides script contracts, compilation, execution, UI state inspection, and basic interactions. Host-specific view names, business APIs, and operation sequences belong in the host’s business scripts.

New scripts are created under Assets/Editor/AutorunScripts/ in the host project and registered after Unity compilation. A useful script answers four questions:

PartWhat it must describe
Starting stateRequired scene, UI, and business state, checked before actions
ActionsVerified host APIs and observable conditions to wait for
DependenciesReused scripts and the parameters explicitly passed to them
AssertionsObservable results that establish the requested goal

Every business script declares Preconditions and overrides CheckPreconditions. A wrong start fails before actions; the runner does not guess a different route. Dependency checks detect missing scripts, duplicate IDs, cycles, and undeclared calls.

Reuse requires the same starting conditions, complete actions, and results. Opening inventory from a login screen and opening it from the home screen are different flows, even though they share a destination. They need separate IDs and source files. Generating a new flow never authorizes changing a reused dependency or weakening its starting conditions.

Prepare Play Mode before a cold-start flow

A cold-start root script declares PreparePlayMode=true. The runner enters Play Mode before checking the script’s actual starting scene and UI. The business script also declares and calls the start-play-mode basic dependency to verify preparation. In Edit Mode, the panel presents Start Game & Run for such scripts.

A child’s declaration does not implicitly turn its parent into a cold-start flow. Initial preparation may continue across the Domain Reload caused by entering Play Mode because no business actions have run. An already running C# iterator cannot resume across a reload: unexpected recompilation or a Play Mode change records a failure without replaying completed actions.

Install and connect

The tool requires Unity 2021.3 or newer, Git, and the .NET 8 SDK. In Unity Package Manager, choose Add package from git URL...:

After import and compilation:

  1. Open Window > Auto Run Window.
  2. Expand Connection > MCP Settings & Diagnostics and use Tools > Publish MCP to build the current server.
  3. Under Install, select the project’s .codex or Claude Code .claude directory, then install MCP and Skills. Existing installations may show Update Skills.
  4. Optionally install or update the separate host Agent Rules entry.
  5. Reconnect the AI client. Check that the Bridge is running and inspect the component versions and installation states.

The installation controls come from the current program in the isolated demonstration project. Client installation targets and the host project’s Agent Rules are separate destinations.

Install Skills installs three self-contained packages. Codex uses .agents/skills/ beside the selected .codex directory; Claude Code uses .claude/skills/. The installer validates and stages the batch, rolls back failed replacements, and refuses to overwrite newer installed versions. Claude Desktop supports MCP installation through its configuration directory, but does not load these filesystem Skills there.

When upgrading, publish the server again and update the Skills and Agent Rules as needed. The old unity-autorun Skill is preserved for manual review and removal so customizations are not deleted. Its retired navigation instructions should not remain the current workflow. Existing scripts in Assets/AutorunScripts/Editor/ remain discoverable, while new scripts use Assets/Editor/AutorunScripts/.

Generate, maintain, and run have separate scopes

SkillResponsibility
gen-scriptCreate an authorized new flow, compile it, self-test it, and repair only code created by that task
edit-scriptMaintain a specified existing business script while preserving its starting state, complete flow, parameters, and goal contract
run-scriptInspect and execute an existing script without generating or modifying code

For example, requests can look like this:

The names and business details in these requests are examples, not APIs or scripts supplied by the tool. The AI must inspect the actual host project before using them.

Generation and editing allow up to three repair rounds by default. Editing includes inspecting dependencies and affected callers, waiting for an available idle runner and completed compilation, and regression-testing affected callers from their declared starts. It cannot change reused dependencies or basic scripts to fit the task. A different starting state, flow, or goal needs a separate generated script.

In the editor, select a script under Autorun Scripts and run it. Expand Run Options for string-valued JSON parameters and timeout, Script Details for source and dependencies, and result/history sections for logs and artifacts. Cold-start preparation follows the root declaration; other scripts expose Start game first as an explicit option.

External execution uses get_script_guidance, list_scripts, and get_script for inspection, then start_script and get_script_status for a tracked run and its terminal result. A new self-test uses a fresh runId; only transport retries of the same execution reuse an ID. Compilation success alone does not establish that the requested test passed.

Check existing coverage before creating a self-test

The separate Install Agent Rules / Update Agent Rules action writes instructions into AGENTS.md at the host Unity project’s root. It is intended for agents that read that project’s rules file, and its destination does not depend on the selected client installation directory.

The rule is straightforward: before game or UI actions for self-testing, use list_scripts and get_script(includeSource=true) to inspect the starting state, complete flow, assertions, parameters, and dependencies. Run a valid matching script directly with run-script. If none matches, explain the missing coverage and ask whether the user wants a self-test script created. Do not silently generate one. An explicit creation request already authorizes creation, so it needs no repeated confirmation.

An unavailable MCP connection, Unity, or Bridge blocks discovery; it does not prove that no script exists. A wrong start or invalid dependency is a blocked test, not a reason to quietly substitute another flow.

The managed instructions use the fixed HTML comment markers unity-autorun:agent-instructions:begin and unity-autorun:agent-instructions:end, with a block version. Updates replace only that block and preserve other user rules. Matching content needs no rewrite. Duplicate, missing, or reversed markers, and newer installed versions, prevent an update instead of overwriting the file.

Open the host’s configuration from a script

Some tests require checking project settings before a run. A business script can expose a configuration entry by providing a public static string ConfigurationMenuPath property with a public getter. Its value is an existing host [MenuItem] path:

Replace the example with a verified menu in the actual project. After compilation and a script-list refresh, selecting that script shows “打开配置界面” (Open configuration) above the run action. Clicking it invokes the host menu. An omitted or empty path hides the action; invalid detected property types/getters or getter failures produce registration errors, and a menu that cannot execute reports its path.

This configuration window belongs to the demonstration project. The host supplies its contents and save behavior; it is not a built-in business settings screen. Run Options separately controls parameters and timeout for one execution.

Keep evidence and preserve the game state

A click being sent does not prove that a panel opened. get_ui_state and wait_for_ui_state inspect supported structured UI properties, but they do not replace business assertions or establish that animation and layout look correct on every device. Visual evidence still requires inspecting actual screenshots.

The screenshot basic script waits for a complete rendered PNG before recording its artifact. Omitting path saves to Temp/UnityAutorunTool/Screenshots/ in the host project. Before the next default capture, cleanup tries to delete files last written more than 24 hours ago and makes room for the new screenshot, aiming to retain the latest 20 files. Locked files or permissions can prevent complete cleanup; this is not a background timer.

An explicit path does not trigger that cleanup. For long-term evidence, specify a unique project-relative .png path outside the tool’s temporary directory. Files there are not included in the temporary cleanup, and an existing destination fails rather than being overwritten. Old screenshots under AutorunToolData/Screenshots/ are not automatically moved or cleaned.

Success, exceptions, timeouts, and cancellation preserve the current game state and Play Mode. Stopping the game is an explicit action. The runner does not automatically reset the scene, roll back the UI, or replay finished steps. A script’s own exit path releases only resources that invocation owns.

For each self-test, I want the actual compilation result, terminal run state, and goal assertions. If the required start, dependency, or caller regression cannot be checked, the report should say what remains unverified and why. That makes the next run useful without turning missing evidence into a success claim.

The tool still serves the same everyday need: remove repeated operations and leave more time for the issue being investigated. C# scripts now keep the preconditions and expected results with those actions, so the next self-test can reuse the whole flow.

Project: Unity-Autorun-MCP. Consult the matching version’s README for current installation instructions and interfaces.

entry.title: Investigating System Freezes Caused by Long-Running Tuanjie Editor Sessions
entry.content:
Over the past couple of days, while developing with Tuanjie, I found that leaving the editor running overnight could freeze my PC. There was no blue screen or consistent error dialog, only occasional OOM errors. I usually had to force a reboot.

After investigation, the root issue turned out to be a memory leak inside Tuanjie itself, which currently also exists on the Unity 6 mainline. Certain paths can trigger it more frequently and eventually cause a freeze. This article records the investigation process.

Environment

  • Operating system: Windows 11
  • Editor: Tuanjie 2022.3.62t6
  • Build branch: tuanjie/1.8/staging

Logs

Because the system was almost completely frozen when the issue occurred, I checked not only Tuanjie’s own logs but also the system crash logs to see whether a child process had unusually high usage.

I asked GPT to scan the drive and found 60 resource-exhaustion events within one week. The most important one was Event ID 2004; both the official documentation and the event description indicated that the crashes were indeed caused by insufficient memory:

Interestingly, these events did not all have the same cause:

  1. In one case, Tuanjie’s private memory grew from about 35.18 GiB to 39.25 GiB, making it highly suspicious.
  2. In another case, system commit reached about 94.93/94.94 GiB.
    • svchost grew to 50.74 GiB.
    • Processes related to DoSvc used about 12.65 GiB.
    • Tuanjie used about 9.08 GiB.

Below are two representative Event ID 2004 entries. I added digit separators to the byte counts to make them easier to review.

The exported system logs contained 83 Event ID 2004 entries in total, with 60 occurring in the preceding seven days.

In the first entry, Tuanjie was clearly the largest consumer.

The second entry was quite different: svchost was the process consuming the largest share.

That made the situation more complicated. Tuanjie was suspicious, but it was not the only explanation for every OOM event. The eventual crash could be the result of multiple memory-leak bugs. The immediate goal was to eliminate the most damaging factor, or at least keep the editor from crashing after being left idle for too long.

Investigation Tool

I had AI put together a MemoryLeakTracker. Its purpose was to collect the following information when system memory showed abnormal growth over a period of time:

Collected dataToolPolicy
System memory and kernel poolsPerformance countersEvery 15 seconds, retained in a rolling buffer
Tuanjie memory, handles, and threadsPerformance countersPreserved when a threshold is reached
Handles, heaps, and virtual-memory stacksWPR/ETWRetains about 10 minutes of ETL data
Process stateProcDumpCreates a dump when private memory reaches 12 GiB
Supporting evidenceEvent logs and system snapshotsSaves one copy before and after the event

The collector is triggered when any of the following conditions is met:

  • Tuanjie private memory exceeds 6 GiB.
  • System commit exceeds 70%.
  • Handle count exceeds 10,000.
  • Growth exceeds 768 MiB within 10 minutes.
  • Private memory reaches 12 GiB, at which point a dump is created.

This tool does not prevent the system from crashing or rebooting. It only needs to leave some final evidence before that happens, so that the next time I log in I can see more specific logs. Without an ETL trace and a dump, all you get is a technically correct but unhelpful statement such as “usage is very high.” With call stacks, there is at least a chance to trace the issue back to the code above DuplicateHandle.

Reproducing the Issue

Once the tool was ready, I restarted the editor and left it running. Surprisingly, the tool displayed its recording prompt after only a few minutes. The reason the crash might normally take days to appear is probably that this machine has 64 GiB of physical memory to absorb the growth for a while.

1. Reproduction

The first important capture was located at:

E:\MemoryLeak-Capture\Incidents\20260720-142209-PID22848

At 14:21:19, two AssetImportWorker processes started.

At 14:22:09, one worker process reached about 11,590 handles, triggering the automatic capture.

The automatically generated incident-20260720-142210.json contained these key fields:

At that point, system commit was only 29.05%, so this was not an active OOM condition. The tracker had caught the abnormal behavior early.

The main process showed a very typical handle pattern: a rising and falling sawtooth curve, with each trough ending higher than the previous one:

TimeMain-process handle count
14:22:106,060
14:24:1835,684
14:29:57120,037
14:30:298,846
14:38:51132,168

From 14:59:59 to 15:00:04, only five seconds elapsed, yet the handle count grew from 14,884 to 16,825 while private memory was still around 4 GiB.

This essentially established the direction of the investigation: the leak was in handles rather than heap memory.

2. Analysis

Next, I used Sysinternals Handle to inspect PID 27308, the process that had just exhibited the problem.

One snapshot contained the following data:

  • Total handles: 97,998.
  • Thread handles: 92,490.
  • Live threads: 289.

The relevant Handle output was as follows:

More than ninety thousand Thread handles is frankly alarming.

After aggregating by target thread, more than 99% of the abnormal handles pointed to TID 30960. In other words, this entire pile of handles was associated with one thread; the system had not actually created that many running tasks.

I strongly suspected that the service behind thread 30960 was being duplicated or restarted repeatedly, causing the handle count to keep growing.

3. Confirmation

To analyze the ETL trace, I installed the Windows Performance Toolkit and loaded Microsoft and Tuanjie symbols in WPAExporter.

In only 15 seconds, the same duplication stack appeared 219,368 times, which was already far beyond normal.

The aggregate summary exported from WPA was:

At this point, the case was essentially solved:

  1. The background loading thread in PreviewTextureManager was executing preview work.
  2. It attached a native thread to Mono through ProtectedScopedThreadAttach.
  3. Mono duplicated the native thread handle.
    • Call site: mono_threads_open_native_thread_handle.
  4. The handles were not closed promptly, so the same thread object accumulated more and more of them.

The root cause therefore lay inside the Tuanjie engine, on the path between the preview thread and the Mono attachment process.

Why Was This Project So Easy to Trigger?

We had found who was leaking, but the investigation was not over. Why did the same engine trigger the issue so frequently in this project?

The editor logs showed that the following file was repeatedly detected, written, and imported around the time the abnormal behavior began:

Following the logs and the code revealed that frequent writes from the ThunderFire UXTool favorites feature were responsible:

  1. RecentSelectRecord subscribes to Selection.selectionChanged.
  2. Whenever the selection changes, the code first removes the old record and then adds a new one.
  3. Both removal and addition call JsonAssetManager.SaveAssets.
  4. SaveAssets writes JSON into the Assets directory.
    • It uses File.WriteAllText.
  5. The write triggers an Asset Database refresh.
  6. Resource items in the “recently selected” panel also call AssetPreview.GetAssetPreview.
  7. These preview requests ultimately enter the leaking PreviewTextureManager.

The Editor-prev.log from before the restart confirmed the same pattern. Here is a short extract:

The prematurely finalized messages line up with the sharp drops in handle count. The finalizer reclaims a batch of objects, but the same creation path is still running.

The key source locations include:

  • RecentSelectRecord.cs: subscribes to selection changes and removes or adds records.
  • RecentFilesSetting.cs: saves JSON immediately after every modification.
  • AssetItemMatFile.cs: requests material previews.
  • AssetItemOthersFile.cs: requests other resource previews.
  • SwitchSetting.json: stores the switch for the “recently selected panel history” feature.

Putting the relevant code together makes the relationship clear:

UXTool is only the trigger. It refreshes and requests previews frequently, but the underlying defect remains in the Tuanjie engine.

Official Issue Record

Unity’s Issue Tracker contains a similar record: UUM-141036.

Its native call chain is almost identical:

However, Tuanjie is an independent branch, so Unity’s work may no longer apply to it. Whether the target version has actually fixed the issue still needs to be verified in practice. Since upgrading the engine in the middle of a project carries substantial risk, this issue may remain with us for quite a long time.

Mitigation

Since I could not fix the issue itself, I disabled the tool that triggers it. I turned off UXTool’s “recently selected panel history” feature and restarted Tuanjie:

Verification

Because the issue had been confirmed to involve handles, I focused on handle counts after the restart:

TimeHandle countPrivate memory
15:45:425,5133,629.7 MiB
15:50:575,8113,702.5 MiB
15:55:576,1003,711.8 MiB
16:03:106,0753,719.1 MiB

During startup, the handle count peaked at 7,564 and quickly fell back to 5,500-6,100.

In a 39-second sample, the handle count grew from 5,831 to 5,871, or about 1.03 handles per second.

After about seven minutes, the count fell again from 6,100 to 6,075.

The old process used to grow by hundreds of handles per second and could spike into the hundreds of thousands. It appears that we removed the main trigger. Given that the underlying issue is in Tuanjie itself, a small residual increase is not surprising. Reducing the frequency of crashes counts as a success.

The Handle summary after restarting was back within the normal range:

Summary

To summarize the chain of events:

  • Surface symptom: repeated memory exhaustion, desktop-component crashes, or a complete system freeze.
  • Confirmed defect: PreviewTextureManager repeatedly duplicates thread handles and does not release them promptly.
  • Project-side trigger: UXTool’s “recently selected” feature repeatedly writes JSON, refreshes assets, and requests previews.
  • Temporary mitigation: disable that feature, exit normally, and restart Tuanjie.
  • Verification: handle growth dropped from 380-400 per second to about 1 per second.
    • Thread handles dropped from 92,490 to 557.
    • The original leak signature disappeared.
  • Long-term resolution: wait for or verify a Tuanjie engine fix. The project-side workaround should not be mistaken for the engine defect having disappeared.

entry.title: Unity Skinned Bounds and Adaptive Display Model Scaling
entry.content:
For collection and leaderboard displays, characters and held models must fit a fixed space. Clothing and item combinations are too numerous to tune individually, so I limited their overall size using bounds.

Some characters then shrank into tiny dots. The scaling formula looked correct; the real problem was the “model size” supplied to it.

Establish what to measure

The display needs the space occupied by participating models in a specified pose. This need not match the mesh asset’s original size or imported bounds covering several animations.

Unity provides several easily confused values:

DataCoordinate spaceDisplay considerations
Mesh.boundsMesh-localOriginal skinned vertices do not represent the current animated pose
SkinnedMeshRenderer.localBoundsRenderer-localMay be a conservative animation envelope rather than a tight fit
Renderer.boundsWorld-space AABBAffected by rotation, skinning updates, and culling
A mesh from BakeMeshRenderer-localA snapshot of the current skinned pose; transformations still need care

During the first investigation, the drawn box was much larger than the character. The size limiter treated that inflated box as the real model and kept shrinking the character.

Cropped from the original Scene view to retain only the character-to-bounds size relationship.

Moving the camera farther away does not fix measurement. It changes projection, while an incorrect measured size still makes the limiter shrink the model improperly.

The first attempt: BakeMesh

SkinnedMeshRenderer.BakeMesh produces a snapshot of the current skinned mesh. When static bounds are too conservative, comparing the baked mesh with Renderer bounds helps determine whether the discrepancy comes from an asset envelope or the current pose.

Do not simply treat mesh.bounds.size as a world size after baking. In a general hierarchy, transform the local box’s eight corners into a common coordinate space and combine them into a new AABB.

Two common mistakes are:

  • Multiplying local size by lossyScale and ignoring rotation’s effect on the world AABB.
  • Baking with scale included, then applying the same scale again in a later matrix transformation.

Our project has an additional complication: clothing bones are rebound to the character skeleton, so the Renderer node’s scale and actual skinning do not always follow a simple hierarchy relationship. Applying “local box times Transform” can collapse the result to a point or inflate it unexpectedly.

I therefore did not settle on BakeMesh as the final solution and continued examining our skinning updates. Baking provides information, but cannot replace confirming the skeleton and coordinate spaces.

Correct size also requires correct timing

The second issue occurred during loading. The character, clothing, and held item become ready separately; resource changes may also cause the Animator to Rebind. Measuring immediately can capture the bind pose or unstable bones.

The same assets working sometimes and failing at other times is typical of this timing problem. I changed the sequence to:

  1. Wait for the character, clothing, and held item to be ready.
  2. Finish refreshing the animation controller and skeleton.
  3. Pass the rebind frame and evaluate the display pose in a subsequent update phase.
  4. Confirm skinning has updated, then collect participating Renderers.
  5. Combine bounds and calculate uniform scaling.

For this dedicated display character, I evaluate a known Idle pose before measurement:

This changes the current pose, so it suits a display character during initialization, rather than resetting a character currently being played. Measuring Idle only establishes its size in that pose; it cannot guarantee later waving, jumping, or every other animation fits the same space.

Offscreen updating is another measurement condition

Display models often finish loading outside the camera view. Even when resources exist, offscreen culling may prevent expected animation or skinning updates.

I enabled updateWhenOffscreen on the relevant SkinnedMeshRenderers and combined it with a known Animator pose and later-frame measurement to obtain usable world-space bounds in our project. This also avoided reconstructing world bounds for unusual skinning hierarchies myself.

This does not mean one switch instantly makes every model’s Bounds accurate. Check whether the project overrides Bounds, whether the skeleton has stabilized, and whether this frame’s animation and skinning evaluation has actually finished.

Continuous offscreen updates cost time. Our limited number of display objects makes that tradeoff acceptable. For many characters, restrict which objects update and for how long, then check results after restoring culling.

Combine only objects actually displayed

A character hierarchy may contain hidden old parts, inactive held items, and particle effects as well as visible clothing. These can inflate bounds.

Filter before collecting:

Use world-space data for the remaining objects and combine it with Bounds.Encapsulate. Initialize from the first valid Renderer, not a zero-sized box at the world origin; otherwise a model away from the origin includes irrelevant space.

I also record which Renderer supplies each axis’s minimum and maximum. That identifies whether clothing inflated X or a bone-associated part stretched Y, rather than exposing only one huge final number.

Scale uniformly using the tightest axis

Let measuredSize be the current size and targetSize the allowed display space. To shrink oversized models without enlarging small ones:

Reject empty collections, zero dimensions, and non-finite values first. Measure under a consistent initial scale; do not repeatedly multiply a model that has already been scaled.

Uniform scaling preserves the character-to-item proportions, but flat or wide items often hit horizontal limits first. Adjust the display space or configure target boxes by resource category instead of loosening every display’s limits for one model.

This solves a three-dimensional size constraint. Keeping the whole model visible in a perspective-camera UI window also depends on view angle, FOV, and screen projection. A world AABB does not guarantee that the image will never be cropped.

The most useful diagnostic information

Starting with abnormal bounds in mid-June, I traced skeleton rebinding, offscreen updates, and measurement timing. For similar problems, first record the current pose, participating Renderers, each axis’s extreme-value sources, and the loading phase when measurement occurs.

Adjusting only the final scale can temporarily hide the fault. Once the measured object, frame, and coordinate space are correct, the fitting formula is straightforward.

References: Renderer.bounds, SkinnedMeshRenderer.BakeMesh, updateWhenOffscreen.

entry.title: Dynamic Unity Timeline Bindings and Asset Authoring
entry.content:
As Timelines grew, the main scene referenced more animation and presentation assets. Assigning them to a PlayableDirector is convenient for artists, but retaining those references makes the scene carry the dependencies at runtime.

I saved Timeline bindings separately, then loaded and restored them on demand. Artists still author and preview in the scene, with an export step before delivery.

TimelineAsset and bindings are separate

A TimelineAsset stores tracks, clips, and timing. A PlayableDirector normally stores which scene object each track controls.

An AnimationTrack needs an Animator; an ActivationTrack needs a GameObject. Detaching and dynamically reloading the TimelineAsset does not automatically recover the scene objects previously assigned to it.

Two problems therefore need solving together: loading assets on demand and restoring track targets afterward.

Dynamic binding can break direct reference chains from the scene to some assets, but cannot guarantee a specific initial package reduction. Asset grouping and other remaining references still affect packaging; an empty Inspector alone does not establish the benefit.

What to save on export

Each Timeline gets a binding description containing resource information and track targets:

FieldPurpose
Timeline asset path and GUIDLocate it in the editor and check correspondence
Track name and typeFind the track to bind
Target hierarchy pathLocate the object in the scene or under a specified root
Target object nameAid diagnostics and constrained lookups
Object and component typesDistinguish a GameObject binding from a component binding

The data is stored as XML. What matters is recoverable location information without retaining direct references to the original scene objects, rather than XML itself.

A simplified entry looks like this:

The exporter traverses timeline.outputs and reads current targets through director.GetGenericBinding(output.sourceObject). For components it stores the containing object’s path and component type; for GameObjects it stores the object’s own type.

Only after writing the file successfully does it clear the Director’s track bindings and playableAsset. The editor also records Undo and marks changes, so clearing scene references remains reversible.

Recovering references at runtime

Before playback, load the TimelineAsset and description, assign the asset to the Director, then resolve targets back into object references. The core call remains Unity’s own API:

This sketches binding; the outer layer handles loading, aggregates failures, and decides whether playback is allowed. Logging a missing critical track does not make preparation successful.

The current implementation indexes tracks by name. Output track names must therefore be unique within an asset, and renaming requires re-export. Supporting duplicate names would require a more stable identifier instead of overwriting same-name entries.

This tool handles track Generic Binding. References inside clips, including ExposedReference, have their own resolution mechanisms; exporting track bindings does not cover every Timeline dependency.

Build a scene object index

Searching from the scene root separately for every track repeatedly traverses the same hierarchy when several Timelines play. I index scene objects by path and use direct lookups for later bindings. A name index retains collections of duplicate names for auxiliary queries.

The search can be limited to one root or cover loaded scenes. Its scope must match the export convention, especially whether paths are full scene paths or relative paths.

Caches need invalidation. Scene or root changes can rebuild the index, but spawning, destroying, and renaming objects within the same scene can also make it stale. Scene names and handles alone cannot detect these changes; the relevant flows must explicitly clear or refresh the index.

Path binding is readable and easy to diagnose, but relies on a stable hierarchy. Moving a node can leave editor previews working while an old binding file fails. Resaving bindings must become part of asset modification.

Preserve the artists’ authoring flow

The basic Timeline editing process stays the same; export and readback are added between saving and integration:

  1. Assign the TimelineAsset to an authoring Director in an appropriate scene.
  2. Select the scene Director, bind targets, and record animation.
  3. Preview the result and save modified animation assets first.
  4. Export bindings through the Director’s menu.
  5. Confirm the file exists and the Director’s references are cleared, then save the scene.
  6. To edit again, reassign the Timeline and read the bindings to restore the authoring state.

Clicking a TimelineAsset in Project and selecting a Director in the scene are different entry points. Recording scene objects requires the latter; otherwise binding or recording may be unavailable.

Not every Timeline needs an extra file. If a complete sequence lives inside one prefab with no references to external scene objects, retain its internal bindings and load the prefab directly. Extra descriptions mainly address resource-to-scene boundaries.

Return control after playback

Loading and binding only establish that a sequence can start. Restoring objects such as cameras afterward also belongs in authoring acceptance checks.

The camera convention then required Timeline-specific cameras to be inactive on the final frame, preventing them from retaining the view after normal completion. Projects should also check ActivationTrack end settings and camera-system priority rules.

For interruption, the last frame is insufficient. The outer stop flow must restore the camera, clean up the Director, and release dynamic assets. Natural completion is only one exit path.

Verify the whole round trip

After implementing the tool, I documented saving, readback, and runtime loading together and required regression testing of existing Timeline playback entry points. New sequences playing successfully do not prove old assets survive reference separation intact.

For a deliverable asset, I would at least test “author → export → read back → play at runtime → complete or interrupt.” This finds mismatched paths and track names, unsaved animation, and cameras that are not released.

Dynamic binding keeps assets visible and editable during authoring while allowing independent runtime loading. Code and authoring conventions must be delivered together to sustain that workflow.

References: PlayableDirector.GetGenericBinding, PlayableDirector.SetGenericBinding.

entry.title: Implementing Action Synchronization with Pass-Through States in Unity Mecanim
entry.content:
Recently, our company launched a casual mini-game, and I handled the animation part. I developed a basic yet functional action synchronization solution based on broadcasting states, without third-party plugins. It suits games that are not sensitive to latency.

The principle is not complicated, and the solution can be set up quickly. What works best is what fits the needs, so I would like to share the thought process behind building it.

Basic Introduction

Unity’s built-in animation system is called Mecanim, which is a state machine-based animation system. Each Layer maintains an active State, which holds animation clips (motion), and the animation clips of the active state are played. Multiple Layers are stacked according to masks to achieve the final animation effect.

There are various ways to play an animation for a state: in addition to setting transition conditions in the AnimatorController for Unity to handle automatically, you can also use the CrossFade API to manually force playback:

Thus, a relatively straightforward solution is to synchronize the local animation state that is currently playing along with its related information, allowing other clients to receive this information and reproduce the action locally using CrossFade, thereby achieving basic animation synchronization.

However, the above is an ideal description; directly adopting this solution in practice can lead to many issues. Below, I will discuss the detailed design based on this synchronization solution and how to avoid these problems to make it truly usable.

Author’s Note:

The goal of this approach is to synchronize animation presentation, not to provide authoritative gameplay synchronization.
The receiving side does not participate in local state decision-making; it is only responsible for consuming the synchronized result.

This makes it suitable for scenarios where the purpose is to let other players see what you are doing, but not for cases where animation timing directly determines gameplay outcomes.

For example, it works well for social emotes, item-holding visuals, and non-critical interaction animations.
However, it is not suitable to rely on this approach directly for things like attack hit detection, fighting game startup frames, or hit stun / stagger reactions.

Solution Details

Synchronize Parameters or State?

If multi-device synchronization is achieved through message forwarding, the most intuitive approach is to broadcast the local AnimatorController’s Parameters, and use the same AnimatorController across multiple devices, somewhat akin to frame synchronization, ensuring consistent results by maintaining input uniformity.

This approach itself isn’t problematic, but considering real-world network latency, directly broadcasting parameters becomes less viable—sending order != receiving order. For the same state machine, different sequences of parameter changes can lead to entirely different outcomes, causing the receiving end’s state to become inconsistent.

Of course, using a cache queue to ensure message order can avoid timing issues, but executing animation states in the Animator also takes time, making it difficult for the receiving end to determine when to fetch new data from the cache, which is quite cumbersome!

In contrast, under the premise of not pursuing strict temporal consistency, broadcasting State appears to be more reliable. Although timing issues still exist, since it is a result-to-result transmission, the “one misstep leads to another” situation seen with parameter broadcasting won’t occur. Additionally, the receiving end no longer needs to consider action execution time, as the sending end will relay the latest state that can be directly reached.

However, simply broadcasting state also has significant limitations. Mecanim’s State can hold more complex substructures (like an Idle-Move-Run blend tree based on speed values), which often require additional data (like speed values) to perform correctly.

Therefore, my approach is to broadcast both the StateNameHash and continuous parameters (such as the speed parameter controlling the Move-Run blend) to achieve basic synchronization. Note that not all parameters in the Animator need to be synchronized; I recommend operating as follows:

TypeRecommended to SyncExample
Continuous parameters driving behaviorRecommendedSpeed, direction, aim pitch, upper body weight
Discrete parameters used only for local decisionsUsually not to sync directlyTrigger, combo index, local bool
Context parameters affecting state interpretationSync as neededWeapon type, posture type, vehicle type

Below is a reference for a data structure using the Protobuf protocol:

[^Note:]: The CrossFade API requires a target state to include at least the state (StateNameHash) and layer (AnimLayer), so both must be included in the broadcast data.

You will notice that the State information sent in the broadcast is divided into three parts. In addition to the current Playing state’s StateNameHash, it also includes the NextStateNameHash for the next state and the StateNormalizedTime for the time already played in the current state. These additional parameters are not mandatory; they are intended to optimize performance and reduce latency, and they relate to Unity Mecanim’s transition mechanism. For detailed explanations, please refer to here.

Sending Local Player Data

Having determined the data to synchronize, we also need to consider the timing for sending the data synchronization. As the project expands, the parameters and states in the AnimatorController will gradually increase, and clearly, we cannot broadcast all states every frame, as this would lead to significant bandwidth consumption.

To make synchronization more precise, I am using a container caching + next frame forwarding approach, as illustrated in the following code:

You can see that the code implements multiple processes. By default, the system will not transmit any data. Only when the m_ThisFrameSyncRequestLayers cache contains data will the animation data for the corresponding layers be sent in the next frame. Whenever a player performs an action (such as using an item), simply call the function shown below to update the cache, and the synchronization system will handle it automatically.

[^Note]: The reason for sending data in the next frame is to wait for the Animator’s state update.

We have eliminated most scenarios; in fact, we can further cache the forwarded state to prevent continuously broadcasting the same state.

Receiving Player Data Synchronization

The receiving end’s processing logic needs to address two main issues: asynchronous initialization and state consistency checks.

Since the timing of network messages may arrive before the player entity’s initialization is complete, the receiving end cannot immediately apply the animation data. The system uses an asynchronous waiting mechanism to process the data only after the target player’s AnimatorController component is ready.

Once the Animator is ready, we do two things:

  1. First, we set the continuous parameters of the Animator (such as speed parameters), which are crucial for states that require continuous value control, like blend trees.
  2. Next is the state consistency check: the system compares the local current state and the next state with the state hash in the broadcast data. If they match exactly, it skips the update to avoid unnecessary animation replay, which can significantly reduce the overhead of repeated synchronization in stable states.

Here is a reference for the basic version of the code:

至此, 我们打通了从发送到接收的大致流程.

Puppet Receiver

I don’t know if you’ve actually followed the above approach and tried it out, but if you did, you would realize that directly applying your AnimatorController to the Player on the receiving end (other players) doesn’t work.
